chapters.title: Opening digression: reinforcement learning and the course scope
chapters.summary: The lecture opens with the missing bell as an analogy to Pavlovian conditioning and reinforcement learning, contrasting it with modern LLMs based on Transformers and neural networks. The instructor then frames the course as Digital Design and Computer Architecture: learning how computers work from transistors upward, including CPUs, GPUs, memory, and machine-learning hardware.

chapters.title: Administrative introduction: instructors, teaching team, and research group
chapters.summary: The instructor introduces his background at ETH Zürich, Carnegie Mellon, Microsoft Research, UT Austin, Michigan, and industry, then presents the co-instructor and head teaching assistants. He also describes the research group’s interests, alumni, newsletters, interviews, and the relevance of research topics such as prefetching, homomorphic encryption, hardware security, and processing-in-memory.

chapters.title: Motivation: designing fundamentally better computers and choosing design metrics
chapters.summary: The instructor argues that the goal of architecture is to enable fundamentally better computing systems, using MIPS R2000 and in-order pipelined processors as historical examples. He introduces key design metrics—performance, energy, cost, robustness, security, reliability, usability, and sustainability—and explains fail-fast design and redundant execution as approaches to handling unreliable hardware.

chapters.title: Transformation hierarchy and cross-layer computer architecture
chapters.summary: The lecture introduces the transformation hierarchy from problems and algorithms down to electrons, devices, logic, microarchitecture, ISA, system software, and programming languages. The instructor motivates an expanded view of computer architecture based on cross-layer design, where algorithms, software, hardware, and devices are co-designed for performance, efficiency, robustness, and security.

chapters.title: Course goals, learning philosophy, and assessment components
chapters.summary: The instructor explains the course goals: understanding computers from the ground up, learning principles and precedents, evaluating design trade-offs, implementing a simple microprocessor in labs, debugging hardware, and developing critical thinking. He describes lectures, readings, homework, labs, exams, extra credit, and advises students to focus on long-term learning rather than only exam preparation.

chapters.title: Why computing exists and how the hierarchy maps problems to electrons
chapters.summary: The lecture returns to the purpose of computing: solving problems and gaining insight, citing Richard Hamming’s view that computing is about insight rather than number crunching. It then formalizes the hierarchy from algorithms and programming languages to system software, ISA, microarchitecture, digital logic, devices, and the physics of electrons.

chapters.title: Definition of computer architecture and examples of computing platforms
chapters.summary: Computer architecture is defined as the science and art of designing computing platforms and hardware-software interfaces to meet specific design goals. Examples include supercomputers, mobile systems, general-purpose machines, self-driving cars, data centers, TPUs, GPUs, wafer-scale chips, genomics accelerators, and processing-in-memory systems.

chapters.title: Break
chapters.summary: The instructor pauses the lecture for a short break and jokes about whether the room bell will ring on time.

chapters.title: Processing-in-memory recap and reasons to study computer architecture
chapters.summary: After the break, the instructor summarizes processing-in-memory chips and broader industry movement toward hardware-software co-design for better efficiency and performance. He explains why architecture matters: enabling better systems, adapting to workloads and technologies, supporting new applications like AI and VR, and addressing problems such as power, memory bottlenecks, programmability, reliability, and security.

chapters.title: Top-down and bottom-up innovation in hardware and software
chapters.summary: The instructor contrasts innovation at the top of the stack—algorithms and software—with innovation at the bottom—devices, materials, and circuits—using Richard Feynman’s “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom” and the idea that there is also room at the top. He emphasizes that the course is not just about hardware but about system design, including hardware-software interfaces, microarchitecture, and concepts such as pipelining, out-of-order execution, and prefetching that also apply in software.

chapters.title: Administrative logistics: course resources, labs, readings, and extra credit
chapters.summary: The teaching staff, assistants, Moodle, office hours, course website, lab attendance, partner selection, FPGA board constraints, prior-year lab grades, final exam, and optional homework are explained. Reading assignments from the textbooks are assigned for the fundamentals, and an extra-credit assignment asks students to watch a research talk on RowHammer without using AI tools.

chapters.title: Fundamentals roadmap: computation, communication, storage, and digital design
chapters.summary: The technical material begins by defining the core components of a computer: computation, communication, and storage or memory, with a later connection to von Neumann principles. The instructor previews the course sequence: transistors, combinational logic, Boolean algebra, sequential logic, hardware description languages, timing, verification, ISA, assembly, microarchitecture, CPUs, GPUs, and memory systems.

chapters.title: General-purpose versus special-purpose processing and hardware platforms
chapters.summary: The instructor distinguishes flexible general-purpose processors from efficient but inflexible special-purpose accelerators, using adjustable wrenches as an analogy and LLM specialization as another example. He describes modern heterogeneous SoCs containing CPUs, GPUs, neural engines, caches, FPGAs, ASICs, and video accelerators, and compares microprocessors, FPGAs, and ASICs in programmability, performance, prototyping, and customization; the course labs will implement a small microprocessor on an FPGA using Verilog.

chapters.title: Administrative introduction: agenda, readings, and extra credit rules
chapters.summary: The lecture opens with the plan to build from transistors to logic gates, combinational logic, and Boolean algebra. The instructor reminds students about reading assignments and the extra credit deadline, emphasizing that AI-generated submissions will receive zero because the goal is to learn the underlying abstractions.

chapters.title: Motivation for transistors and transistor-count scaling
chapters.summary: The instructor explains that modern digital computers are built from transistors, contrasting them with hypothetical mechanical or biological computers. Examples from the Intel 4004, Pentium 4, Apple M2 Max, and flash memory illustrate the enormous growth in transistor counts and the importance of semiconductor fabrication.

chapters.title: MOS transistors as voltage-controlled switches
chapters.summary: A MOS transistor is introduced as a device with gate, source, and drain terminals; applying a voltage to the gate controls whether source and drain behave like a wire or an open circuit. NMOS and PMOS transistors are compared using the wall-switch analogy: NMOS turns on with high gate voltage, while PMOS turns on with low gate voltage.

chapters.title: CMOS logic gates and the CMOS inverter
chapters.summary: Because NMOS pulls down well and PMOS pulls up well, modern circuits use complementary MOS, or CMOS. The simplest CMOS gate, the inverter or NOT gate, is derived from one PMOS pull-up transistor and one NMOS pull-down transistor, with its voltage behavior mapped to binary logic and a truth table.

chapters.title: Construction of NAND, AND, and NOR gates from CMOS transistors
chapters.summary: A two-input NAND gate is built from PMOS transistors in parallel and NMOS transistors in series, and its truth table is derived case by case. The AND gate is obtained by adding an inverter to a NAND gate, NOR is described by swapping series/parallel arrangements, and NAND/NOR are noted as logically complete.

chapters.title: General CMOS gate structure, invalid states, and latency
chapters.summary: The general CMOS structure uses a PMOS pull-up network and an NMOS pull-down network, with exactly one network on at a time to avoid short circuits or undefined floating outputs. The instructor explains why series transistor stacks are slower than parallel connections due to resistance and mentions pseudo-NMOS and other tricks to reduce latency.

chapters.title: Dynamic power, static power, energy, and total design power
chapters.summary: Power consumption is split into dynamic power from switching capacitances and static power from leakage current, with voltage, capacitance, and frequency all affecting energy use. The lecture distinguishes energy from maximum power or total design power, discusses power gating, voltage-performance-reliability trade-offs, and briefly mentions Dennard scaling during Q&A.

chapters.title: Common logic gates, Moore’s Law, and semiconductor manufacturing
chapters.summary: The instructor reviews common gates such as buffer, XOR, XNOR, and multi-input NAND, then connects transistor scaling to Moore’s Law. Moore’s 1965 prediction, manufacturing cost trends, heat removal, lithography, materials, and newer device technologies are discussed as the foundation enabling modern computer architecture.

chapters.title: Break and optional Moore paper review
chapters.summary: The instructor recommends reading Moore’s paper as an optional review exercise and then calls an approximately eleven-minute break. There is brief classroom logistics about the bell and returning from break.

chapters.title: Definition of combinational logic circuits and functional specification
chapters.summary: After the break, the lecture defines logic circuits in terms of inputs, outputs, functional specification, and timing specification. Combinational circuits are introduced as memoryless systems whose outputs depend only on current inputs, in contrast to sequential circuits that also depend on stored history; a one-bit full adder is used as an example Boolean specification.

chapters.title: Boolean algebra axioms, duality, simplification, and De Morgan’s laws
chapters.summary: Boolean algebra is reviewed as an algebra over 0 and 1 using AND, OR, and NOT, with commutative, identity, distributive, complement, associative, and duality laws. Simplification theorems and De Morgan’s laws are connected to circuit minimization, gate substitutions, area, latency, energy, and electronic design automation tools.

chapters.title: Canonical sum-of-products form and minterm notation
chapters.summary: The lecture introduces canonical representations so a truth table can be translated into a standardized Boolean expression. Sum-of-products form is derived by OR-ing all minterms whose output is 1, with terminology such as literal, implicant, minterm, and decimal minterm indices explained; the nonminimal nature of canonical SOP is contrasted with simplified forms like A + BC.

chapters.title: Product-of-sums form, maxterms, complements, and conversions
chapters.summary: Product-of-sums form is presented as the dual canonical form that uses output-0 rows, expressing a function as an AND of maxterms. The instructor explains minterm-to-maxterm conversion, complementing a function by swapping output zeros and ones, and notes that exams and exercises often require Boolean simplification from SOP or POS forms.

chapters.title: Combinational blocks and construction of a decoder
chapters.summary: The lecture moves from gates to reusable modules, emphasizing abstraction: once a block such as an adder is understood, it can be treated by its function. A decoder is defined as an input-pattern detector with n inputs and 2^n outputs, and a 2-to-4 decoder is built from the truth table using AND gates and complemented inputs.

chapters.title: Applications of decoders in memory addressing and instruction decoding
chapters.summary: The instructor explains why decoders are useful: they select a row in a memory array from an address and activate the correct circuit for an instruction. Instruction bit patterns for operations such as ADD, XOR, and multiply are decoded to control the appropriate hardware units, demystifying part of processor operation.

chapters.title: Definition and implementation of multiplexers
chapters.summary: A multiplexer, or selector, is introduced as a circuit that connects one of several data inputs to an output based on select lines. A 2-to-1 multiplexer is specified by a truth table and implemented using AND, OR, and NOT gates, then a 4-to-1 multiplexer is shown both as two-level logic and as a tree of 2-to-1 multiplexers.

chapters.title: Using multiplexers as lookup tables in FPGAs
chapters.summary: Multiplexers are shown to implement arbitrary logic functions by treating the truth table as a lookup table and using function inputs as select lines. Examples include AND, XOR, an arbitrary three-input function, and a three-input majority function, motivating FPGA lookup tables and programmable logic.

chapters.title: Decoder-based logic functions and wrap-up
chapters.summary: The instructor briefly notes that decoders combined with OR gates can also implement Boolean functions by generating minterms and selecting the needed ones. An XNOR example is mentioned, and the lecture closes by saying the next lecture will continue with the full adder.

chapters.title: Student announcement: Start Hack hackathon
chapters.summary: Students present an announcement for Start Hack 2025, described as a large European hackathon with hundreds of participants and case partners across finance, government, AI, and drone-related projects. They encourage students to apply soon and emphasize teamwork, practical problem solving, and the event being free to participants.

chapters.title: Opening remarks and recap of combinational logic
chapters.summary: The lecture opens with informal remarks and a roadmap: finish combinational logic, then introduce memory and sequential logic. The instructor reviews gates, Boolean equations, truth tables, sum-of-products/product-of-sums forms, logic minimization, and why different Boolean implementations affect area, latency, power, and energy.

chapters.title: Review of decoders, multiplexers, and lookup tables
chapters.summary: Decoders are reviewed as input-pattern detectors with one active output, and multiplexers as selectors that route one data input to an output. The instructor also recalls multiplexer trees, implementing logic with multiplexers and decoders, and FPGA lookup tables.

chapters.title: Derivation of a one-bit full adder from a truth table
chapters.summary: The instructor derives binary addition for one bit using inputs A, B, and carry-in, producing sum and carry-out. The carry-out is identified as a three-input majority function, while the sum is a three-input XOR; both are also constructed mechanically from truth-table minterms in sum-of-products form.

chapters.title: Ripple-carry adder and carry-lookahead adder trade-offs
chapters.summary: A one-bit full adder is composed into a four-bit ripple-carry adder, where each carry must propagate serially to the next stage. The instructor then introduces carry-lookahead adders as an optimized design that uses extra specialized carry-generation logic to reduce latency, illustrating the area–latency trade-off.

chapters.title: Q&A on adder layout conventions and timing sources
chapters.summary: Students ask whether adders have a fixed left-to-right or right-to-left drawing convention and what determines latency. The instructor explains that drawing conventions vary and that timing depends on both gate delays and wire delays, to be revisited in timing and verification.

chapters.title: Programmable Logic Array implementation of sum-of-products logic
chapters.summary: A Programmable Logic Array is introduced as a universal two-level implementation for any N-input, M-output combinational function using an AND array followed by an OR array. The full adder is revisited as a PLA example by programming connections from minterms to the sum and carry OR gates.

chapters.title: Logical completeness of AND/OR/NOT, NAND, and NOR
chapters.summary: The instructor explains logical completeness: because any truth table can be expressed in sum-of-products form, AND, OR, and NOT can implement any Boolean function. NAND and NOR are also stated to be logically complete, with students encouraged to prove this using Boolean transformations.

chapters.title: Comparator design as an equality checker
chapters.summary: After noting optional readings on arithmetic blocks, the instructor presents an N-bit comparator that checks whether two values match bit by bit. A four-bit equality comparator is built efficiently using XNOR gates and an AND gate, contrasting it with a much larger truth-table/PLA implementation.

chapters.title: Arithmetic Logic Unit design and modular datapath functions
chapters.summary: An Arithmetic Logic Unit is introduced as a block that selects among arithmetic and logical functions such as AND, OR, addition, subtraction, and set-less-than based on function-select inputs. The implementation is analyzed as a divide-and-conquer composition of adders, inverters, multiplexers, and control signals, including a discussion of overflow and modular design.

chapters.title: Tri-state buffers, shared buses, and multiplexer implementation
chapters.summary: Tri-state buffers are introduced as enabled switches that either drive a wire or leave it floating. They are used to explain shared CPU–memory buses, bus contention hazards, and cheaper multiplexer implementations using tri-state buffers instead of conventional AND/OR gate structures.

chapters.title: Break and transition to logic simplification
chapters.summary: The instructor pauses for a break and then resumes, joking about the unreliable bell. The next section is framed as a quick tour of logic simplification before moving to sequential logic.

chapters.title: Boolean simplification and the uniting theorem
chapters.summary: The full adder SOP implementation is revisited as expensive logic that can be simplified to XOR and majority functions. The instructor explains automated Boolean simplification through the uniting theorem: if an input changes while the output remains 1, that input can be eliminated from the expression.

chapters.title: Priority circuit with don't-cares and Karnaugh map mention
chapters.summary: A fixed-priority requester/grant circuit is used to show how don't-care entries compact a truth table and reduce hardware. The instructor distinguishes the priority circuit from a decoder, notes that the simplification embodies the uniting theorem, and briefly mentions Karnaugh maps as a graphical technique not covered in detail.

chapters.title: Introduction to sequential logic and the need for memory
chapters.summary: The lecture shifts from combinational circuits, whose outputs depend only on current inputs, to sequential circuits, whose outputs can depend on past inputs. The instructor motivates memory as central to processors and modern systems, showing examples of SRAM caches, DRAM main memory, and storage technologies.

chapters.title: Cross-coupled inverters as a one-bit storage element
chapters.summary: A pair of cross-coupled inverters is presented as the simplest circuit that can hold one bit, with two stable states Q=1/Q̅=0 and Q=0/Q̅=1. The instructor also introduces metastability as an undesirable condition that can occur when the circuit cannot settle cleanly to one stable state.

chapters.title: Q&A on storage technologies
chapters.summary: A student asks about common storage devices, and the instructor distinguishes flash-based solid-state drives from magnetic hard disks, tape, CD-ROMs, and DVDs. This short discussion places latches, SRAM, DRAM, flash, and other storage technologies on a spectrum of speed, density, cost, and volatility.

chapters.title: Set-reset latch using cross-coupled NAND gates
chapters.summary: The cross-coupled inverter is extended into an SR latch using cross-coupled NAND gates and active-low set/reset control inputs. The instructor explains hold, set, and reset behavior and forbids driving both S and R low because it violates the Q/Q̅ invariant and can cause metastability.

chapters.title: Gated D latch and multi-bit register construction
chapters.summary: To prevent invalid SR latch inputs, two extra NAND gates create a gated D latch with a data input and write-enable signal. Multiple D latches are then placed in parallel to form a register, such as a four-bit register with shared write enable and vector notation for inputs and outputs.

chapters.title: Memory array design with decoders and multiplexers
chapters.summary: Memory is built as multiple addressable registers: a decoder selects which row/location is accessed, and multiplexers select the data read from that row. The instructor constructs two-location and four-location toy memories using gated D latches, address decoders, write-enable gating, and read multiplexers.

chapters.title: Implementing logic with memory lookup tables and sequential lock analogy
chapters.summary: The instructor shows that a memory array can implement Boolean logic by storing truth-table outputs at addresses corresponding to input combinations, as in FPGA lookup tables. The lecture ends by contrasting a combinational lock with a sequential lock to motivate the next topic: state in sequential circuits.

chapters.title: Announcements and plan for sequential logic, labs, and Verilog
chapters.summary: The lecture opens with the plan to finish sequential logic and finite state machines, then hand over to the lab head TA for labs and FPGAs. Administrative notes cover the 1% extra-credit policy and the upcoming topics of hardware description languages, Verilog, timing, and verification.

chapters.title: Review of latches, registers, and memory arrays
chapters.summary: The instructor reviews prior storage elements: cross-coupled inverters, SR latches, gated D latches, registers, and memory arrays. The memory example uses address decoding, read and write enable signals, rows, and data inputs/outputs.

chapters.title: Definition of state using a combination lock
chapters.summary: The lecture introduces state as the information a system must remember about relevant past events. A mechanical combination lock illustrates the difference between combinational behavior, which depends only on current inputs, and sequential behavior, which depends on a history such as R13, L22, R3.

chapters.title: State diagram for the sequential combination lock
chapters.summary: The combination lock is represented as a finite state diagram with states A through D and transitions based on correct or incorrect dial inputs. The discussion explains how wrong inputs return the lock to the initial state and notes assumptions around the open state and relocking.

chapters.title: Asynchronous versus synchronous state transitions and the clock
chapters.summary: The instructor distinguishes asynchronous machines, where state changes immediately in response to inputs, from synchronous machines, where changes occur only at clock events. A traffic light introduces the clock signal, rising edge, falling edge, and clock cycle as the mechanism for synchronizing state transitions.

chapters.title: Clock period, combinational delay, and synchronous design trade-offs
chapters.summary: The lecture explains that in synchronous circuits, combinational logic must finish evaluating within the clock cycle before the next rising edge. It also discusses why synchronous control is easier for large systems, while asynchronous design can avoid clock overhead but is harder to verify and integrate.

chapters.title: Synchronous circuit structures and pipelining
chapters.summary: Several synchronous circuit patterns are shown: combinational logic alone, logic feeding a state element, feedback through state for an FSM, and register-to-register pipelines. The instructor explains that modern processors use pipelining so different stages compute concurrently while registers latch results each cycle.

chapters.title: Definition and components of a finite state machine
chapters.summary: A finite state machine is defined as a discrete-time model of a stateful system with a finite set of states, inputs, outputs, transition rules, and output rules. The hardware organization is introduced as next-state logic, a state register, and output logic.

chapters.title: Required behavior of an edge-triggered state register
chapters.summary: The desired state register behavior is specified: sample the next-state input only at the rising clock edge and hold the current state stable for the whole clock cycle. Timing waveforms show why transient input changes or glitches during the cycle must not immediately change the register output.

chapters.title: Why a gated D latch cannot implement the state register
chapters.summary: A gated D latch connected directly to the clock is shown to be level-sensitive: while the clock is high, changes on D propagate to Q. This violates the FSM register requirement because glitches and mid-cycle input changes can alter the state during the clock cycle.

chapters.title: Construction of a rising-edge D flip-flop from two latches
chapters.summary: A D flip-flop is built from two D latches controlled by opposite clock phases, so the output changes only at the clock edge. The lecture identifies the flip-flop as an edge-triggered storage element and shows how D flip-flops form multi-bit registers.

chapters.title: Moore and Mealy FSMs and smart traffic light controller design
chapters.summary: The instructor distinguishes Moore machines, whose outputs depend only on state, from Mealy machines, whose outputs also depend on inputs. A smart traffic light controller is designed by drawing the transition diagram, encoding states, building the state transition table, deriving Boolean next-state equations, and constructing output logic.

chapters.title: FSM practice example and general FSM design procedure
chapters.summary: A tape-reading snail example is suggested for further practice with Moore and Mealy FSM design. The lecture summarizes the design flow: determine all states, develop the transition diagram, define inputs and outputs for each state, choose a reset state, and implement the resulting logic.

chapters.title: Break and transition to lab and FPGA lecture
chapters.summary: The class takes a break and then reconvenes for the lab head TA’s presentation. The instructor introduces the remaining session as an overview of lab logistics and FPGAs.

chapters.title: Lab logistics, grading, reports, partners, and AI policy
chapters.summary: The TA explains lab schedules, partner work, FPGA board distribution, grading of ten labs, in-lab demonstrations, lab reports, late penalties, and reuse of previous lab grades. A tentative AI policy emphasizes doing the labs with one’s partner, understanding the work well enough to explain it, and using AI only cautiously for issues such as obscure tool errors.

chapters.title: Learning goals of the labs: processors, HDL, debugging, and trade-offs
chapters.summary: The labs will connect the transformation hierarchy to hands-on digital design by implementing and debugging hardware. Students will use Verilog and CAD tools, prototype on FPGAs, and learn performance-versus-area trade-offs while building toward a processor.

chapters.title: What FPGAs are and where they fit among processors and ASICs
chapters.summary: FPGAs are introduced as reconfigurable integrated circuits whose functions, interconnects, and I/O can be configured to implement digital circuits. The TA positions FPGAs between general-purpose CPUs/GPUs and special-purpose ASICs in programmability, performance, and energy efficiency.

chapters.title: FPGA applications in acceleration, testing, prototyping, and field updates
chapters.summary: The lecture surveys FPGA use cases, including Microsoft deep learning inference, Amazon F1 instances, bioinformatics accelerators, climate modeling, DRAM testing infrastructures, RowHammer studies, in-DRAM computation, flash characterization, architecture prototyping, CERN systems, trading, medical imaging, and space computing. The examples motivate FPGAs as platforms for workload acceleration, system characterization, research prototypes, and updatable deployed hardware.

chapters.title: Course FPGA board and overview of the lab sequence
chapters.summary: Students will use a Basys-style FPGA board to learn microprocessor design in Verilog and eventually build a small 32-bit processor. The lab sequence includes basic circuits, comparison, sequential circuits, an ALU, testing, assembly programming, image manipulation, processor design, a Snake program, and adding instructions for performance.

chapters.title: FPGA architecture: configurable logic blocks, routing, and connection boxes
chapters.summary: The TA explains the main FPGA fabric: configurable logic blocks, lookup tables, switch boxes, connection boxes, interconnect, and I/O blocks. Routing is implemented using configuration memory controlling pass transistors or tri-state buffers, with area and signal-quality trade-offs.

chapters.title: Lookup tables and modern FPGA resources
chapters.summary: A lookup table is shown as a multiplexer selecting programmed truth-table values, and a 3-input LUT example implements a majority function that outputs one when at least two inputs are one. The lecture then shows how large designs combine many LUTs and notes modern FPGA resources such as flip-flops, carry units, on-chip memory, high-speed I/O, memory interfaces, and embedded processors.

chapters.title: FPGA advantages, disadvantages, Verilog-to-Vivado flow, and final lab reminders
chapters.summary: The TA summarizes FPGA benefits—hardware specialization, lower development cost than ASICs, short time to market, and field reconfiguration—and drawbacks such as lower speed and energy efficiency than custom chips due to area and latency overheads. The session ends with the lab programming flow: describe designs in Verilog, use Vivado for simulation and implementation, load the generated bitstream onto the FPGA, and follow submission and grading instructions carefully.

chapters.title: Course logistics, recap, and agenda for Verilog
chapters.summary: The lecture opens with attendance comments, a recap of combinational logic, logical completeness of NAND/NOR, sequential logic, and finite state machines. The agenda is hardware description languages, implementing combinational logic, implementing sequential logic/FSMs, and preparing for labs and later microprocessor design.

chapters.title: Motivation: learning fundamentals before relying on automation
chapters.summary: Using Salvador Dalí paintings as an analogy, the instructor argues that students should learn basic design principles before using or ignoring them. This is connected to AI-generated programming or hardware design: without understanding the underlying principles, one cannot judge correctness, usefulness, or efficiency.

chapters.title: Why hardware description languages are needed
chapters.summary: Modern processors, GPUs, memory chips, and wafer-scale systems contain billions to trillions of transistors, creating a major complexity challenge. HDLs provide a way to specify, simulate, and synthesize hardware, and are preferred over general-purpose languages because hardware has explicit concurrency, wires, gates, flip-flops, clocks, and edges.

chapters.title: Hierarchical hardware design: modules, top-down, and bottom-up
chapters.summary: Hardware complexity is managed by dividing designs into modules such as cores, caches, memory controllers, multiplexers, decoders, and ALUs. The lecture explains top-down design from a microprocessor to submodules, bottom-up design from leaf cells and technology libraries, and why both are used in practice.

chapters.title: Verilog module definitions, ports, buses, slicing, and syntax
chapters.summary: The instructor introduces Verilog modules as the main building blocks, with names, input/output ports, internal wires, and module bodies. The chapter covers bus declarations, bit ranges, indexing conventions, bit slicing, concatenation, replication, assignment statements, case sensitivity, identifiers, whitespace, and comments.

chapters.title: Structural Verilog and gate-level multiplexer implementation
chapters.summary: Two HDL implementation styles are introduced: structural HDL, which connects gates and module instances, and behavioral HDL, which describes function. The lecture shows structural module instantiation, explicit versus positional port connections, and a 2-to-1 multiplexer built from primitive NOT, AND, and OR gates.

chapters.title: Behavioral combinational Verilog: operators, multiplexers, constants, and tri-state buffers
chapters.summary: Behavioral HDL is presented as a higher-level way to describe combinational circuits using logical, bitwise, reduction, arithmetic, and conditional operators. Examples include Boolean expressions, bitwise NAND/NOR/XOR, reduction AND, 2-to-1 and 4-to-1 multiplexers with ternary operators, operator precedence, numeric constants in different bases, floating Z values, and tri-state buffers.

chapters.title: Synthesis, simulation, and the HDL design mindset
chapters.summary: The lecture distinguishes synthesis, which maps synthesizable HDL to gate-level netlists and cell libraries, from simulation, which checks behavior before implementation. The instructor stresses that HDL should be treated as a description of hardware, not as an ordinary computer program, and recommends sketching combinational blocks, registers, and FSMs before coding.

chapters.title: Break and announcement: Tiny Tapeout chip-design opportunity
chapters.summary: After a short break, Frank from the electrical engineering department announces the CIS CHIPS / Tiny Tapeout project, where students can submit small open-source chip designs for free fabrication and a board. The announcement covers the webinar, submission deadline, open-source tools and technology, IP ownership, and examples such as gates or multiplexers.

chapters.title: Abstraction tradeoffs, comparators, parameterized modules, timing annotations, and style guidelines
chapters.summary: Returning from the announcement, the lecture compares low-level versus high-level Verilog styles using a 4-bit equality comparator, progressing from XNOR and AND gates to concise equality expressions. It then introduces parameterized modules for reusable designs, simulation-only timing delays, and coding guidelines such as consistent naming, MSB-to-LSB bus ordering, one module per file, and remembering that Verilog describes hardware.

chapters.title: Sequential Verilog: clocks, always blocks, and D flip-flops
chapters.summary: Sequential logic is introduced as combinational logic plus memory, requiring constructs for clocks, edges, flip-flops, latches, and FSM state. The instructor defines the Verilog always block and shows a D flip-flop using always @(posedge clock), a reg output, and a nonblocking assignment.

chapters.title: Reset, enable, and latch descriptions in Verilog
chapters.summary: The lecture explains reset signals for initializing FSMs and hardware to a known state, contrasting asynchronous reset with synchronous reset and noting issues such as glitches and metastability. It then implements D flip-flops with asynchronous reset, synchronous reset, enable/write-enable, and finally a level-sensitive latch described with an always block sensitive to clock and data.

chapters.title: When always blocks describe combinational versus sequential circuits
chapters.summary: The instructor summarizes always-block rules and shows that an always block may describe either sequential or combinational hardware depending on sensitivity lists and whether all outputs are assigned in all cases. Examples demonstrate unintended latches from incomplete assignments or missing sensitivity-list signals, and introduce case statements, default cases, and casez/casex-style don't-care matching for combinational logic.

chapters.title: Blocking versus nonblocking assignments and Verilog coding rules
chapters.summary: The lecture distinguishes nonblocking assignments, where updates occur concurrently at the end of a block, from blocking assignments, where statements execute in order. It applies the distinction to sequential logic and a carry-generation example, then gives coding rules: use nonblocking assignments in clocked always blocks, continuous assignments for simple combinational logic, always @* with blocking assignments for more complex combinational logic, and never assign the same signal from multiple always blocks or continuous assignments.

chapters.title: Announcement: semester speaker feedback channels
chapters.summary: The semester speaker introduces himself and the contact route for questions, complaints, and suggestions, which can be forwarded to Professor Mutlu. The instructor encourages students to use these channels for positive or negative feedback.

chapters.title: Lecture roadmap: HDL wrap-up before timing and verification
chapters.summary: The lecture is introduced as the start of timing and verification, with a preview that next week will raise the abstraction level to computer architecture and the von Neumann model. Before moving on, the instructor reviews hardware description languages, Verilog, sequential circuits, and the need to think about hardware parallelism and clocks.

chapters.title: Finite state machine structure and divide-by-three clock divider design
chapters.summary: The instructor reviews the three components of a finite state machine: state register, next-state logic, and output logic. A simple three-state FSM is designed to divide a clock frequency by three, with state S0 as the reset state and the only state where output Y is high.

chapters.title: Verilog implementation of the divide-by-three FSM
chapters.summary: The divide-by-three FSM is described in Verilog using state and next-state registers, parameterized state encodings, an active-high asynchronous reset, combinational next-state logic, and combinational output logic. The example is identified as a Moore-type FSM because the output depends only on the current state.

chapters.title: Q&A: clock division for energy savings and synthesis results
chapters.summary: A student asks why one would divide a clock frequency; the answer connects frequency reduction to dynamic power and energy savings, including voltage scaling. Another question discusses whether different Verilog descriptions might synthesize to different circuits, emphasizing that synthesis and technology mapping determine area and optimization details.

chapters.title: Example: smiling snail sequence detector FSM for 1101
chapters.summary: The instructor revisits the “smiling snail” sequence detector that outputs a smile when the last four bits seen are 1101. Moore and Mealy implementations are compared: the Moore machine uses five states, while the Mealy machine uses four states because its output depends on both state and current input; the Mealy version is then mapped into Verilog.

chapters.title: Introduction to circuit timing and design trade-offs
chapters.summary: The timing and verification section begins by distinguishing functional correctness from timing correctness. The instructor introduces design trade-offs including area, speed, latency, throughput, frequency, power, energy, design time, and the risk of incorrect results when a circuit is clocked too fast.

chapters.title: Physical causes of delay and definitions of contamination and propagation delay
chapters.summary: The ideal logic abstraction of instantaneous outputs is replaced by the real behavior of gates with finite switching delay caused by capacitance, resistance, voltage, temperature, process variation, and other conditions. Two key delay measures are defined: contamination delay as the minimum delay until an output starts changing, and propagation delay as the maximum delay until it finishes changing.

chapters.title: Critical path and shortest path analysis in combinational circuits
chapters.summary: A combinational circuit example is used to compute the longest delay path, called the critical path, and the shortest delay path, which determines contamination delay. The instructor shows how output nodes change over time as an input transition propagates through gates, and notes that wire delay is temporarily ignored.

chapters.title: Example: propagation delay of four-to-one multiplexer implementations
chapters.summary: The instructor discusses real gate data sheets where propagation delay depends on voltage and temperature, then compares multiple four-to-one multiplexer implementations. Designs using standard gates and tri-state buffers have different critical paths, demonstrating that implementation choices strongly affect delay and that loading and wire capacitance complicate analysis.

chapters.title: Q&A: overclocking, crashes, and wrong latched values
chapters.summary: In response to a question, the instructor explains that overclocking can cause wrong results when a clock edge captures a value before the combinational logic has settled. Higher operating speed can also increase temperature and worsen the chance of timing failures.

chapters.title: Output glitches and Karnaugh-map redundancy fix
chapters.summary: A glitch is defined as one input transition causing multiple output transitions because different paths through a circuit have different delays. The instructor shows how a temporary wrong output can be dangerous if latched into state, and explains that adding redundant logic, visible through a Karnaugh map, can eliminate the glitch at the cost of area, power, and design effort.

chapters.title: Break announcement before sequential timing
chapters.summary: The instructor closes the glitch discussion by reminding students to recognize glitches in simulation and avoid letting them affect state. A short break is announced before moving to sequential circuit timing.

chapters.title: D flip-flop timing constraints and metastability
chapters.summary: Sequential timing analysis begins with an abstract D flip-flop that samples D on a clock edge and outputs Q. Setup time, hold time, aperture time, clock-to-Q contamination delay, clock-to-Q propagation delay, and metastability are introduced as essential timing properties of registers.

chapters.title: Derivation of setup and hold constraints between registers
chapters.summary: The instructor derives timing constraints for a register-to-register path with combinational logic in between. The setup constraint sets a minimum clock period based on clock-to-Q propagation delay, combinational propagation delay, and setup time, while the hold constraint requires the minimum clock-to-Q plus combinational contamination delay to exceed the hold time and is independent of clock frequency.

chapters.title: Worked example: sequential timing analysis and hold-time violation repair
chapters.summary: A sequential circuit with multiple input and output registers is analyzed using given flip-flop and gate timing values. The setup constraint gives a 215 ps minimum clock period and about 4.65 GHz maximum frequency, while the hold constraint fails and is fixed by adding buffers on the short path.

chapters.title: Clock skew effects on setup and hold timing
chapters.summary: Clock skew is introduced as the difference in clock arrival times at different registers due to nonzero clock distribution delay. The instructor derives how worst-case skew increases the effective setup and hold requirements, reduces performance, and motivates balanced clock distribution networks such as H-trees.

chapters.title: Overview of circuit verification and testing challenges
chapters.summary: The lecture shifts to verification: determining whether a circuit is functionally correct and whether it meets timing requirements. The instructor contrasts simulation with formal verification, explains why large digital designs and modern processors are hard to test, and notes that testing dominates the cost of cutting-edge processor design.

chapters.title: Functional verification with Verilog test benches
chapters.summary: Functional verification is presented as logic simulation using test benches that drive inputs to a device under test and check outputs. The instructor describes handcrafted, self-checking, and automatic test benches, automatic test pattern generation, golden designs, and the scalability problem of testing all input combinations.

chapters.title: Closing remarks and next lecture preview
chapters.summary: The instructor stops the test-bench discussion and says testing will continue next week. The next lecture will also move to a higher abstraction level and begin architecture-level topics.

chapters.title: Announcements and recap: timing analysis and design principles
chapters.summary: The lecture opens with reminders about the extra-credit assignment, the no-AI rule, and an additional verification/testing lecture. The instructor reviews sequential-circuit timing analysis, clock-cycle time, critical paths, balanced design, pipelining, common-case design, and Amdahl's Law as the final bridge from digital design.

chapters.title: Motivation for verification, testing, and robust systems
chapters.summary: Functional and timing verification are distinguished, with emphasis on why timing verification is difficult across voltage, temperature, workload, and manufacturing conditions. Examples such as RowHammer, RowPress, voltage droop, and silent data corruption motivate online testing and the need for reliable, safe, secure, and predictable systems.

chapters.title: Course transition from digital design to ISA and microarchitecture
chapters.summary: The instructor marks the end of the digital-design portion and introduces the next abstraction level: the execution model and the instruction set architecture as the hardware/software interface. The plan is to study the von Neumann model, MIPS, LC-3, assembly programming, and later microarchitecture implementations.

chapters.title: Definition of a computer, program, instruction, and instruction set
chapters.summary: A modern computer is described as processing logic, memory, and communication mechanisms such as I/O and interconnects. A program is defined as a set of instructions, where each instruction specifies a well-defined unit of work, and the instruction set is the complete set of operations a machine is designed to perform.

chapters.title: Definition of the von Neumann execution model
chapters.summary: The von Neumann model is introduced as the dominant execution model, with memory, processing unit, input, output, and control unit. Its key behavioral idea is sequential execution in program order, a model followed by major ISAs such as x86, ARM, MIPS, and RISC-V.

chapters.title: Memory organization: address space, addressability, bytes, and words
chapters.summary: Memory is defined as a bit array that stores both programs and data, grouped into bytes and architecture-dependent words. The instructor explains address space, byte addressability, word addressability, and examples from LC-3, MIPS, and x86-64.

chapters.title: Endianness in byte-addressable memory
chapters.summary: The lecture explains how a multi-byte word is laid out in byte-addressable memory and uses Gulliver's Travels as an analogy for conventions. Big-endian and little-endian byte order are compared, including the practical issue of converting data between systems with different conventions.

chapters.title: Memory reads and writes using MAR and MDR
chapters.summary: The instructor describes how a processor accesses memory using a memory address register and memory data register. Read and write sequences are broken into steps involving loading the MAR, transferring data through the MDR, and respecting memory latency and control signals.

chapters.title: Processing unit and ALU operations specified by the ISA
chapters.summary: The processing unit is introduced as the component that performs computation through functional units such as ALUs. LC-3 and MIPS are compared in terms of operations such as ADD, NOT, XOR, subtract, multiply, shifts, and set-less-than, illustrating how ISA choices affect hardware and software complexity.

chapters.title: Registers and the register file as fast temporary storage
chapters.summary: Registers are motivated as fast storage near the ALU to avoid repeatedly accessing slow memory for intermediate values or reused variables. The instructor defines architectural registers, register files, word-sized registers, LC-3's eight general-purpose registers, MIPS's thirty-two registers, and the special hardwired-zero register convention.

chapters.title: Input, output, and memory-mapped I/O
chapters.summary: Input and output devices are introduced as the way information enters and leaves a computer, with examples such as keyboards, monitors, disks, and printers. LC-3 will use keyboard and monitor examples and briefly introduce memory-mapped I/O, where device registers are accessed like memory locations.

chapters.title: Break
chapters.summary: A short break is announced before continuing with the control unit and the rest of the von Neumann model.

chapters.title: Control unit, instruction register, and program counter
chapters.summary: After the break, the control unit is described as the orchestrator of instruction execution. The instructor defines the instruction register, program counter or instruction pointer, and programmer-visible architectural state consisting of memory, registers, and the PC.

chapters.title: Stored program and sequential instruction processing
chapters.summary: The two essential von Neumann properties are identified: instructions and data share memory, and instructions are processed sequentially unless control-flow instructions change the PC. The instructor then introduces an LC-3-like datapath with MAR, MDR, register file, ALU, bus, tri-state buffers, PC, IR, and a finite-state control unit.

chapters.title: Instruction storage, fetching, sample program, and instruction formats
chapters.summary: Instructions and data are shown as memory contents, with the PC selecting the next instruction and advancing by one word or by the instruction length in bytes. A sample MIPS program illustrates assembly code versus machine code, and instructions are defined as having an opcode plus operands, with LC-3 examples of ADD instruction encoding.

chapters.title: Operate instructions: ADD and AND in LC-3 and MIPS
chapters.summary: Operate instructions are introduced as ALU instructions, using A = B + C as the high-level example mapped to registers in LC-3 and MIPS assembly. The instructor explains LC-3 register-register ADD and AND encodings, decoder use for opcodes, register-file source and destination fields, and the MIPS R-type format with opcode, rs, rt, rd, shamt, and funct fields.

chapters.title: Memory operations: load word and base-plus-offset addressing
chapters.summary: Load and store instructions are motivated as the way to move operands between memory and registers. The load-word example explains base-plus-offset addressing for arrays, LC-3 LDR encoding with a six-bit offset, MIPS load-word encoding with a sixteen-bit immediate, and the difference between word-addressable and byte-addressable machines.

chapters.title: Instruction processing cycle: fetch, decode, address, execute, and store result
chapters.summary: The instruction cycle is decomposed into phases: fetch, decode, evaluate address, fetch operands, execute, and store result, noting that not every instruction uses every phase. The LC-3-style datapath is used to trace fetching into the IR, opcode decoding with a 4-to-16 decoder, address calculation for LDR, ALU execution for ADD, and writing results back to registers.

chapters.title: Control-flow instructions: jump and changing the PC
chapters.summary: The lecture ends by introducing control instructions that break the default sequential PC progression. An LC-3 jump instruction is shown as loading the PC from a base register during execute, while MIPS jump is briefly mentioned before the next lecture continues with more instruction details.

chapters.title: Announcements and roadmap for ISA and microarchitecture
chapters.summary: The lecture opens with attendance comments, an extra-credit reminder, and a roadmap: finish ISA trade-offs, connect ISA to assembly programming, and begin implementing an ISA as a microarchitecture using logic blocks.

chapters.title: Review of ISA concepts and the LC-3b instruction processing cycle
chapters.summary: The instructor reviews instruction formats, opcodes, data types, addressing modes, control-flow instructions, and the six-stage instruction processing cycle. The LC-3b finite-state machine is used to show fetch, decode, and opcode-directed state transitions using the PC, MAR, MDR, and IR.

chapters.title: Program translation: compiler, assembler, linker, loader, and MIPS memory map
chapters.summary: A high-level program is traced through compilation to assembly, assembly to an object file, linking to an executable, and loading into memory before execution begins at the program counter. The MIPS memory map is introduced, including text, static data, dynamic data, and the role of symbol tables and fixed addresses.

chapters.title: Q&A and poll on assembly programming experience
chapters.summary: The instructor asks how many students have programmed in assembly and answers a question about where initialized static variables and their actual values reside in memory. Students are encouraged to study assembly programming for the labs.

chapters.title: ISA trade-off: complex versus simple instructions and the semantic gap
chapters.summary: The lecture turns to ISA design trade-offs, asking how complex instructions, data types, and addressing modes should be. The semantic gap between high-level languages and the ISA is explained: complex ISAs ease software translation but complicate hardware, while simple ISAs shift more work and optimization burden to software.

chapters.title: Indirection with binary translation and implementation ISAs
chapters.summary: An extra level of indirection can expose one ISA to software while translating internally to another, simpler implementation ISA. Examples include Apple Rosetta 2 translating x86 to ARM, Intel and AMD translating x86 instructions into micro-operations, NVIDIA Denver, and Transmeta code morphing to VLIW; virtual memory is previewed as another form of indirection.

chapters.title: ISA trade-off: number of architectural registers
chapters.summary: The number of registers affects instruction encoding size, register allocation quality, memory traffic, register-file latency, area, and power. LC-3’s 8 registers and MIPS’s 32 registers illustrate the trade-off between more fast storage and larger encodings or hardware structures.

chapters.title: Questioning the von Neumann execution model
chapters.summary: The instructor revisits the von Neumann model: stored programs, unified instruction/data memory, a program counter, and sequential instruction processing except at control transfers. The class is prompted to consider whether this dominant model is the only way to process programs.

chapters.title: Definition of the dataflow execution model
chapters.summary: Dataflow execution is introduced as an alternative to program-counter-driven execution. Instructions fire when all input operands are ready, ordering is determined by data dependencies, and many ready instructions can execute in parallel if enough functional units exist.

chapters.title: Dataflow nodes, tokens, and graphical control constructs
chapters.summary: A dataflow program is described as a graph of nodes that fire when input tokens arrive. The instructor shows how an operation can encode opcode, destination, and readiness bits, and introduces conditional, relational, copy, and branch-like nodes for graphical programming or FPGA implementation.

chapters.title: Exercise: reverse-engineering a dataflow factorial program
chapters.summary: A graphical dataflow program with inputs 1 and N, copy nodes, branch nodes, a decrement node, and a multiply node is presented. Students are asked to determine the output value after execution for a nonnegative integer N.

chapters.title: Break
chapters.summary: The class takes a short break after the factorial dataflow exercise prompt, with students asked to think about what the program computes.

chapters.title: Solution: tracing the factorial dataflow graph
chapters.summary: After the break, the class identifies the program as computing N factorial. The instructor traces token flow for N = 4, showing repeated multiplication by N and decrementing until zero, when the final accumulated value is output and the remaining token dies.

chapters.title: Program counter as an ISA execution-model trade-off
chapters.summary: The instructor contrasts ISAs with a program counter, which provide control-driven sequential execution, against dataflow-style ISAs without a PC, which enable data-driven parallel execution. The discussion highlights ease of programming, compilation, performance, parallelism extraction, and hardware complexity as high-level trade-offs.

chapters.title: Using microarchitecture to hide parallel execution under a sequential ISA
chapters.summary: Even if the ISA exposes sequential execution, the microarchitecture can internally execute instructions in different orders or in parallel as long as architectural state changes obey ISA semantics. This separates the programmer-visible contract from the hidden implementation used for performance.

chapters.title: Modern processors preserve von Neumann ISAs while violating them internally
chapters.summary: Most major general-purpose ISAs expose the von Neumann model, but implementations use pipelining, superscalar execution, out-of-order execution, and separate instruction and data caches. These techniques violate the simple one-instruction-at-a-time model internally while preserving the ISA abstraction for software.

chapters.title: Definitions of ISA, microarchitecture, and microprocessor
chapters.summary: The lecture defines ISA as the contract between software and hardware, microarchitecture as a specific implementation of that contract, and a microprocessor as the combination of ISA, microarchitecture, and circuits. The instructor notes that the term architecture is often used imprecisely to mean either ISA or ISA plus implementation.

chapters.title: Implementing an ISA and the gas-pedal analogy
chapters.summary: Microarchitecture is presented as one of many possible implementations of the same ISA, with examples from MIPS, x86, POWER, ARM, Alpha, RISC-V, and IBM Z. The gas-pedal analogy explains that the driver-facing interface can stay the same while the internal engine implementation varies widely.

chapters.title: Backward compatibility and what ISA versus microarchitecture specifies
chapters.summary: The instructor explains why ISAs change slowly: programs depend on backward compatibility, so vendors usually add instructions rather than remove or radically change old ones. The ISA specifies visible behavior such as instructions, memory, exceptions, access control, I/O, and multiprocessor behavior, while microarchitecture covers hidden choices such as pipelining, clock gating, and error correction.

chapters.title: Exam practice: classifying ISA and microarchitecture properties
chapters.summary: Students classify features as ISA or microarchitecture properties: opcode and number of general-purpose registers are ISA-visible, while adder type, multiply latency, and register-file port count are implementation choices. The program counter is emphasized as part of the ISA execution model.

chapters.title: Design points and application-driven computer architecture trade-offs
chapters.summary: A design point is defined by constraints and priorities such as cost, performance, power, energy, reliability, availability, time to market, and target applications. Different markets—scientific computing, mobile processors, machine-learning accelerators, CPUs, GPUs, and domain-specific accelerators—lead to different ISA and microarchitecture trade-offs.

chapters.title: Computer architecture as science and art under uncertain futures
chapters.summary: The instructor argues that architecture is both science and art because future applications, users, markets, and technologies cannot be fully predicted. Building reuse analogies from Zurich and Pittsburgh illustrate that systems designed for one purpose may later be used for another, motivating flexible trade-offs; the lecture closes by recommending the assembly programming material and previewing microarchitecture next time.

chapters.title: Announcements and roadmap for microarchitecture lectures
chapters.summary: The co-instructor introduces himself, notes Professor Mutlu is traveling, and previews the sequence of topics: single-cycle, multicycle, pipelined, and later more modern processor designs. Reading suggestions are mentioned, with the caveat that standard books become less adequate for modern processors.

chapters.title: Definition of microarchitecture and architectural state
chapters.summary: Microarchitecture is recalled as the hardware implementation of an ISA under design goals and constraints, hidden from software as long as ISA semantics are preserved. The lecture defines processing an instruction as transforming architectural state AS into AS′ according to the ISA, and relates the ISA to an abstract finite-state machine.

chapters.title: Single-cycle versus microarchitectural intermediate states
chapters.summary: Two implementation choices are contrasted: directly moving from AS to AS′ in one hardware cycle, or using hidden microarchitectural states across multiple cycles. The LC-3 instruction-processing FSM is used as an example of the second approach, while the rest of the lecture focuses on the single-cycle choice.

chapters.title: Combinational implementation and critical path of a single-cycle processor
chapters.summary: A single-cycle processor must fetch, decode, read operands, execute, access memory, and write results using combinational logic between clocked state elements. Its clock period is determined by the longest instruction path, so even simple instructions must wait for the latency of the slowest instruction.

chapters.title: Comparison of single-cycle and multicycle machines
chapters.summary: Single-cycle machines update architectural state only at the end of one long cycle, while multicycle machines break instruction processing into stages with hidden intermediate state. In multicycle machines the slowest stage, not the slowest whole instruction, determines clock cycle time, giving more design flexibility while preserving von Neumann semantics.

chapters.title: Six phases of instruction processing
chapters.summary: The lecture lists the fundamental instruction-processing phases: instruction fetch, decode, address evaluation, operand fetch, execution, and result storage. In a single-cycle design all phases fit in one cycle, whereas a multicycle design may allocate one or more cycles to each phase.

chapters.title: Datapath and control logic as processor components
chapters.summary: Instruction processing is described as transforming input data into output data through functional units. The datapath contains ALUs, registers, memories, buses, multiplexers, and wires, while control logic generates signals that tell the datapath what to do; the LC-3 datapath/control diagram is used for illustration.

chapters.title: Processor design space and performance equation
chapters.summary: The design methodology is outlined: build a single-cycle datapath, analyze its weaknesses, then improve it with multicycle, pipelined, and eventually out-of-order designs. Performance is introduced using execution time = instruction count × average CPI × clock cycle time, with examples showing tradeoffs among algorithms, ISA complexity, CPI, and microarchitecture.

chapters.title: Q&A on historical single-cycle processors and design tradeoffs
chapters.summary: In response to a question, the instructor notes uncertainty about whether real historical processors were truly single-cycle, suggesting the design is mainly pedagogical and that early processors were generally multicycle. The discussion reinforces why single-cycle designs have fixed CPI but poor clock-cycle flexibility, unlike multicycle processors.

chapters.title: MIPS state elements: PC, register file, and memories
chapters.summary: The single-cycle design target is a simplified MIPS processor with a 32-bit program counter, 32-bit instructions, 32 general-purpose registers, separate instruction and data memories, and read/write control signals. The register file has two read ports, one write port, 5-bit register specifiers, 32-bit data paths, and a RegWrite enable.

chapters.title: Memory-array notation and single-cycle memory assumptions
chapters.summary: The lecture connects the MIPS register file and memories to earlier memory-array structures built from decoders and multiplexers. For the single-cycle design, it assumes ultra-fast combinational reads and synchronous writes for memories and register files, while noting that realistic memories may require ready signals, as in LC-3b.

chapters.title: Five-stage view and initial single-cycle datapath skeleton
chapters.summary: The six processing phases are collapsed into five practical steps: instruction fetch, decode/register operand fetch, execute/address calculation, memory access, and writeback. A basic datapath skeleton is introduced with PC to instruction memory, register file reads to the ALU, ALU output to data memory or writeback, and data memory output back to the register file.

chapters.title: Break and scope of the simplified MIPS subset
chapters.summary: The instructor pauses for a break and previews that the rest of the lecture will add logic to the datapath. The design will cover enough MIPS instructions to explain the principles, but not the full MIPS ISA.

chapters.title: Datapath support for R-type ALU instructions
chapters.summary: R-type MIPS instructions such as add rd, rs, rt are explained using their opcode, rs, rt, rd, shamt, and funct fields. The datapath routes instruction bits 25–21 and 20–16 to the register-file read ports, bits 15–11 to the write-register port, uses the ALU operation selected by the function code, and writes the ALU result back with RegWrite asserted.

chapters.title: Datapath support for I-type ALU instructions
chapters.summary: I-type ALU instructions such as addi use one source register, one destination register, and a 16-bit immediate that is sign-extended to 32 bits. Two multiplexers are added: one to choose the destination register field, and one to choose between the second register operand and the sign-extended immediate as the ALU input.

chapters.title: Datapath support for load word and store word
chapters.summary: Load word computes a memory address by adding a base register to a sign-extended offset, reads data memory, and writes the result to rt; store word computes the same kind of address and writes register data to memory. Additional datapath paths and a writeback multiplexer select between ALU results and memory read data, while MemRead, MemWrite, and RegWrite are controlled appropriately.

chapters.title: Unconditional jump datapath and target address formation
chapters.summary: The MIPS jump instruction is described as using a 26-bit target field combined with the upper four bits of PC+4 and two low zero bits, because instructions are word-aligned in byte-addressed memory. A mux is added to choose between PC+4 and the jump target, and the instructor highlights the common mistake of using PC instead of PC+4 for the upper bits.

chapters.title: Jump-and-link variants and conditional branch datapath
chapters.summary: Other jump instructions such as jump register, jump and link, and jump and link register are briefly introduced, especially for function calls and returns. Conditional branches such as beq compute a PC-relative target from PC+4 plus a sign-extended, shifted offset, and use the ALU zero flag after subtraction to decide whether to take the branch.

chapters.title: Delayed branch semantics in MIPS
chapters.summary: MIPS delayed branch semantics are previewed: the instruction immediately after a branch executes regardless of whether the branch is taken. The instructor notes this was motivated by pipelining but is often inconvenient because compilers may struggle to fill the delay slot usefully.

chapters.title: Complete single-cycle datapath with branch and jump PC control
chapters.summary: The assembled datapath includes adders, multiplexers, sign extension, shift-left-two logic, register file, ALU, memories, and PC-selection logic. Branch control combines the decoded branch signal with the ALU zero output to choose the branch target, while jump control overrides the PC path for unconditional jumps.

chapters.title: Hardwired control logic and instruction-specific signal settings
chapters.summary: The lecture explains how hardwired control can be derived from opcode and function fields without building an impractically huge truth table, using semantic definitions and Boolean equations for signals such as RegDst and ALUSrc. It then walks through control settings and datapath flows for R-type, I-type, load, store, branch-not-taken, branch-taken, and jump instructions, noting don't-care conditions and mentioning microprogrammed control as an alternative.

chapters.title: Performance evaluation of the single-cycle microarchitecture
chapters.summary: The instructor assigns students to review the datapath construction and begins evaluating whether single-cycle design is good. Using example component latencies, the load word instruction is shown to have the longest path at 600 ps, forcing the single-cycle clock period even though other instructions are faster; control logic latency is noted as a possible critical-path contributor in larger ISAs.

chapters.title: Closing remarks and Persian New Year announcement
chapters.summary: The lecture ends with a note that the performance discussion will continue next week. The instructor wishes students a nice weekend and mentions Persian New Year, briefly noting its mathematical and physical basis.

chapters.title: Announcements and agenda: from single-cycle to multicycle and pipelined processors
chapters.summary: The lecture opens by framing the continuation of microarchitecture design: finishing the single-cycle datapath/control discussion, then moving to multicycle processor design and possibly pipelining. Readings are mentioned from Harris and Harris Chapter 7.4 and Patt and Patel appendices, with later lectures expected to cover pipelining issues and out-of-order execution.

chapters.title: Review of single-cycle performance and slow memory
chapters.summary: The instructor reviews the single-cycle MIPS-style microarchitecture, where every instruction must take as long as the slowest one, such as a load word. The recap emphasizes that real memory is slow, instructions require at least an instruction fetch, and some instructions may need multiple memory accesses, making single-cycle timing unrealistic.

chapters.title: Problems with single-cycle design and violated microarchitecture principles
chapters.summary: Single-cycle design is criticized for forcing all instructions to run at worst-case latency, duplicating combinational resources, and becoming impractical for complex instructions. The lecture introduces critical-path design, common-case or “bread-and-butter” design, and balanced design, showing that single-cycle processors violate all three principles.

chapters.title: System design principles: simplicity and low cost
chapters.summary: A short aside connects computer architecture to broader system-design principles: design should be based on principles rather than precedent, kept as simple as possible, and kept low cost. The instructor cites Butler Lampson’s “Hints for Computer System Design” and uses architecture examples to motivate principled design.

chapters.title: Definition and motivation of multicycle microarchitecture
chapters.summary: The lecture introduces multicycle microarchitecture, where the clock cycle time is chosen independently of total instruction processing time and each instruction uses only as many cycles as it needs. This is related to transitions through invisible microarchitectural states between programmer-visible architectural states, as previously seen in the LC-3 finite-state machine.

chapters.title: Benefits and costs of multicycle design
chapters.summary: Multicycle design improves critical-path optimization, common-case optimization, and balanced resource use by allowing different instructions to use different numbers of states and by reusing hardware. Its costs include storing intermediate results in extra registers, paying setup/hold sequencing overhead multiple times, and having limited concurrency because only part of the processor is active in each cycle.

chapters.title: Finite-state-machine control for multicycle processors
chapters.summary: The instructor explains that a multicycle processor can implement instruction processing as an FSM that sequences through states and returns to fetch. Each state corresponds to asserted control signals, and generating next-cycle control signals early avoids lengthening the current cycle’s critical path.

chapters.title: Design goals for the multicycle MIPS datapath
chapters.summary: The multicycle datapath is motivated as a lower-cost alternative to single-cycle MIPS, using one unified memory instead of separate instruction and data memories and one ALU instead of multiple adders. The design process follows the same method as single-cycle design: build datapath support for each instruction, then design the control logic.

chapters.title: Datapath for load word in a multicycle processor
chapters.summary: Using `lw` as the first example, the lecture builds the fetch, decode, address calculation, memory read, and write-back datapath. It introduces the instruction register, register-file operand latches, sign extension, ALU result register, memory data register, and multiplexers needed to share memory and hardware across cycles.

chapters.title: Extending the multicycle datapath for PC update, store, R-type, and branch
chapters.summary: The datapath is extended to reuse the ALU for `PC + 4`, support `sw` by adding a second register-file read path to memory write data, support R-type instructions with destination-register and ALU-source multiplexers, and support `beq` by subtracting operands and computing the branch target from `PC + 4` plus shifted offset. The result is the complete multicycle datapath with extra temporary registers but fewer major functional units than the single-cycle design.

chapters.title: Q&A and break: branch target calculation and branch timing
chapters.summary: A student asks how `beq` uses two registers and the branch target address, leading to clarification that the target can be calculated in one state and the branch condition evaluated in another. The instructor notes that instruction latency can depend on control-state choices, thanks the class, and announces a break before moving to control logic.

chapters.title: Control-unit FSM for fetch and decode states
chapters.summary: After the break, the lecture begins designing the multicycle controller that drives multiplexer selects, register enables, memory write, ALU operation, and PC update signals. The fetch state reads memory using the PC, writes the instruction register, computes `PC + 4`, and updates the PC; the decode state is mostly empty in this datapath because register reads and operand latching occur unconditionally.

chapters.title: Control FSM states for load, store, R-type, branch, add immediate, and jump
chapters.summary: The controller shares states where possible: load and store both use a memory-address state, then split into memory read/write and load write-back; R-type instructions use execute and ALU write-back states; branches compute a target in decode and then evaluate the condition. The datapath and FSM are then extended for `addi` and `j`, including a widened PC-source multiplexer and jump-target concatenation.

chapters.title: Handling variable-latency memory in a multicycle FSM
chapters.summary: The instructor asks what the multicycle design assumes about memory and explains that a simple version assumes single-cycle memory. Unlike a single-cycle processor, a multicycle FSM can handle long-latency memory by staying in a memory-access state until a memory-ready signal is asserted, as in LC-3b-style control.

chapters.title: Introduction to microprogrammed multicycle control
chapters.summary: The lecture introduces microprogramming as a way to view control signals as low-level microinstructions that program the datapath. A high-level ISA instruction can be implemented as a sequence of microinstructions, making complex instructions such as matrix multiplication conceptually feasible through low-level sequencing, loops, and branches.

chapters.title: Microprogram control terminology and controller-store organization
chapters.summary: The instructor defines a microinstruction as the set of control signals for a state, microsequencing as selecting the next microinstruction, and the control store as the memory holding all microinstructions. A microsequencer reads the current microinstruction and datapath/control conditions to choose the next control-store address, allowing branching and looping inside the microprogram.

chapters.title: Microprogramming as an abstraction layer and ISA translator
chapters.summary: Microprogramming is presented as a powerful abstraction: the designer can translate a desired ISA operation into a sequence of existing control signals and add datapath resources only when necessary. The instructor connects this to the semantic gap, where the microsequencer translates high-level ISA instructions into simpler user-invisible microinstructions executed by hardware.

chapters.title: Advantages, patching, and tradeoffs of microprogrammed control
chapters.summary: Microprogrammed control allows a simple datapath to emulate a richer ISA, supports complex instructions, enables ISA extensibility, and permits field updates to fix hardware bugs. Historical examples include IBM 370, IBM System z “millicode,” and Burroughs B1700 user microprogramming, followed by Q&A on abstraction overhead, compiler optimization, and just-in-time compilation analogies.

chapters.title: Motivation for pipelining: limited concurrency in multicycle processors
chapters.summary: The lecture returns to the question “Can we do better?” and identifies limited concurrency as a key weakness of multicycle design: fetch, decode, execute, memory, and write-back resources are often idle in different phases.
