The goal of pipelining is to use otherwise idle hardware to process multiple instructions at once and increase instruction throughput.

chapters.title: Basic pipeline execution and throughput improvement
chapters.summary: Pipelining is introduced using the assembly-line analogy: instruction processing is divided into stages, and different instructions occupy different stages simultaneously. Compared with serial multicycle execution, a full pipeline can complete roughly one instruction per cycle in steady state, reducing average CPI, though later lectures will address pipeline hazards and other issues.

chapters.title: Announcements, readings, and recap of multicycle MIPS
chapters.summary: The lecture plan is to finish basic pipelining, especially data and control dependence handling, while precise exceptions and out-of-order execution are deferred to later lectures. The instructor reviews readings from Harris & Harris and Patterson & Hennessy and recaps single-cycle and multicycle MIPS, including waiting for multicycle memory accesses.

chapters.title: Basic pipeline throughput and the laundry analogy
chapters.summary: Using independent add instructions and laundry loads, the lecture explains how overlapping stages improves throughput to one completed task per cycle in steady state while leaving individual task latency roughly unchanged. The example emphasizes independence between different tasks and distinct resources for different stages.

chapters.title: Pipeline bottlenecks, resource replication, and real assembly-line examples
chapters.summary: A slower dryer illustrates that the slowest pipeline stage limits throughput, and adding another dryer models duplicating a bottleneck resource such as a multiplier. Historical examples from Ford automobile assembly and IBM Stretch show that pipelining is a general and long-standing throughput technique.

chapters.title: Definition of an ideal pipeline
chapters.summary: An ideal pipeline aims to increase throughput with little extra cost and requires repeated identical operations, independence between repeated operations, and evenly partitionable suboperations. The instructor relates these conditions to laundry and prepares to apply them to instruction processing.

chapters.title: Pipeline performance limits: sequencing overhead and hardware cost
chapters.summary: The lecture derives ideal and realistic throughput when combinational logic is split into K pipeline stages, showing that register sequencing overhead limits gains as pipelines become deeper. It also discusses how extra pipeline registers increase hardware cost, so infinitely deep pipelines are neither practical nor optimal.

chapters.title: Five-stage MIPS pipeline partitioning and speedup example
chapters.summary: The single-cycle MIPS datapath is divided into instruction fetch, decode/register access, execute/address generation, memory, and write-back stages. A load-word timing example shows that unequal stage latencies reduce the speedup of a five-stage pipeline from the ideal 5× to about 4×.

chapters.title: Adding pipeline registers and carrying data through stages
chapters.summary: Pipeline registers are inserted between stages, and any value needed later—such as the instruction, PC+4, branch target information, and destination register number—must be carried down the pipeline. The lecture also stresses that multiple instructions occupy different stages simultaneously and that a simple linear pipeline forces all instruction classes through all stages.

chapters.title: Pipeline control signals and propagation through pipeline registers
chapters.summary: Pipeline control reuses the same control signals as the single-cycle design, but the signals must be delayed until the stage that consumes them. Two approaches are introduced: decode once and pipeline the control bits, or carry instruction fields and decode locally; the lecture focuses on the first approach.

chapters.title: Why instruction pipelines are not ideal
chapters.summary: The lecture explains that real instruction pipelines violate all ideal-pipeline assumptions: instructions use different stages, stages have unequal delays, and instructions may depend on each other. These issues create external fragmentation, internal fragmentation, data dependence, control dependence, resource contention, and long-latency operation problems.

chapters.title: Break
chapters.summary: The instructor pauses the lecture and asks students to return at 3:15 before continuing with pipeline stalls and dependencies.

chapters.title: Pipeline stalls and resource contention
chapters.summary: A stall is defined as a condition where the pipeline stops moving, caused by resource contention, dependences, or long-latency operations. Resource contention can be handled by duplicating resources or increasing their throughput, such as using separate instruction and data memories or carefully timing register-file reads and writes within a cycle.

chapters.title: Types of data dependence: RAW, WAR, and WAW
chapters.summary: The instructor distinguishes true flow dependence, or read-after-write, from anti-dependence, or write-after-read, and output dependence, or write-after-write. RAW dependences reflect real producer-consumer relationships, while WAR and WAW are name dependences caused by limited architectural registers and can often be avoided by careful pipeline ordering or register renaming.

chapters.title: Fundamental methods for handling flow dependences
chapters.summary: Six broad strategies are introduced for RAW dependences: detect and wait, forward or bypass data, eliminate dependences in software, move dependent work aside for independent instructions, predict needed values, or execute work from another thread. These methods connect simple in-order pipelines to later topics such as compiler scheduling, speculation, and fine-grained multithreading.

chapters.title: Stalling, bubbles, interlocking, and the MIPS design philosophy
chapters.summary: A dependent instruction can be stalled until its source value is available, while upstream stages are frozen and downstream stages drain by inserting bubbles or NOPs. The lecture introduces software versus hardware interlocking and explains the historical meaning of MIPS: Microprocessor without Interlocked Pipeline Stages.

chapters.title: Hardware detection of data dependences: scoreboarding vs combinational checks
chapters.summary: Two hardware approaches to dependence detection are compared: scoreboarding with a valid bit per register, and explicit combinational logic that compares source registers in decode against destination registers in later stages. Scoreboarding is simpler but stalls for more dependence types, while combinational checking avoids false stalls but grows more complex in deeper or superscalar pipelines.

chapters.title: Data forwarding and bypassing paths
chapters.summary: Data forwarding supplies a producer’s result directly from a later pipeline stage to a dependent consumer, rather than waiting for register-file write-back. The lecture shows ALU-to-ALU forwarding paths from the EX/MEM and MEM/WB stages to ALU inputs, including multiplexers and priority rules when multiple candidate forwarded values exist.

chapters.title: Load-use stalls and hardware support for inserting bubbles
chapters.summary: Forwarding cannot always eliminate stalls, especially for a load-use dependence because the loaded value is only available at the end of the memory stage. The pipeline handles this by disabling the program counter and IF/ID register, clearing or resetting downstream pipeline registers to insert bubbles, and preserving the stalled instruction until it can proceed.

chapters.title: Control dependence and simple branch prediction
chapters.summary: Control dependence is introduced as a dependence on the program counter: the fetch unit must choose the next PC before a branch is resolved. The simplest prediction is always not taken, fetching PC+4 and flushing wrongly fetched instructions if the branch is later found to be taken.

chapters.title: Early branch resolution and more accurate branch prediction
chapters.summary: To reduce misprediction penalty, branch target and condition computation can be moved earlier into the decode stage, but this adds hardware, forwarding needs, and possibly a longer clock cycle. The lecture closes by previewing better branch predictors based on loop direction, branch history, and even machine-learning-style techniques, and assigns the remaining performance examples for self-study.

chapters.title: Announcements and lecture roadmap: precise exceptions, interrupts, and pipelining
chapters.summary: The lecture opens with microphone setup, holiday/break announcements, and a recap of prior coverage of single-cycle and multi-cycle microarchitectures. The instructor previews precise exceptions and interrupts as a bridge from pipelining to out-of-order execution, with readings including the Smith and Sohi paper on superscalar processors.

chapters.title: Problem: variable-latency functional units violate sequential semantics
chapters.summary: The instructor introduces pipelines with multiple functional units whose execution latencies differ, such as integer add, integer multiply, floating-point multiply, and load/store units. A timeline example shows later independent instructions writing back before an earlier divide, exposing out-of-program-order updates to architectural state and violating the von Neumann sequential model.

chapters.title: Exception example: divide by zero, breakpoints, and the need for precise state
chapters.summary: Using divide by zero and debugger breakpoints, the lecture explains why no later instruction should update architectural state after an exception-causing instruction, while all previous instructions should be complete. A tram analogy illustrates an exceptional event that stops normal execution until the exception is handled and possibly resumed.

chapters.title: Definitions and examples of exceptions versus interrupts
chapters.summary: Exceptions are defined as internal to the running program, while interrupts are external events that require processor attention. Examples include divide by zero, overflow, undefined opcode, page faults, I/O device service requests, timer interrupts, power failure, and machine checks.

chapters.title: When and how exceptions and interrupts are handled
chapters.summary: The instructor contrasts handling timing, priority, and context for exceptions and interrupts: exceptions are handled when detected and known to be non-speculative, while many interrupts can wait until a convenient point except high-priority events. Handling requires saving architectural state and transferring control to an operating-system exception or interrupt handler, with possible return to the interrupted program.

chapters.title: Definition of precise exceptions and precise interrupts
chapters.summary: A precise exception or interrupt means architectural state is consistent at the handling point: all older instructions have retired and no younger instruction has updated architectural state. The lecture defines retirement/commit and explains why the clean sequential boundary is the key property needed for correctness.

chapters.title: Pipeline control actions for servicing an exception
chapters.summary: When the oldest instruction is ready to retire, hardware checks whether it caused an exception; if so, it ensures precise state, flushes younger pipeline instructions, saves required state, and redirects the program counter to the appropriate handler. The handler may later restore state and return to the interrupted program if recovery is possible.

chapters.title: Why precise exceptions matter: ISA contract, debugging, restart, and traps
chapters.summary: After citing the x86 architectural description of interrupts and exceptions, the instructor motivates precise exceptions as required by the ISA contract and essential for software debugging. Additional benefits include restartable processes, software traps for unimplemented instructions such as multiply via undefined opcode handling, and support for virtual memory.

chapters.title: Supporting precise exceptions in single-cycle and multi-cycle machines
chapters.summary: Precise exceptions are trivial in single-cycle processors because instruction and cycle boundaries coincide. In multi-cycle processors, the finite-state control machine is extended with special states for exceptions such as overflow and undefined instruction, entered only at precise points before the next instruction is fetched.

chapters.title: MIPS exception datapath: EPC, Cause register, and MFC0
chapters.summary: The MIPS-style datapath is augmented with an Exception Program Counter (EPC), a Cause register, control signals to record the exception reason, and a path to the exception-handler address. The handler can use MFC0 to read the cause, save and restore registers, copy EPC into a general-purpose register such as K0, and jump back when appropriate.

chapters.title: Variable-latency pipelines require hardware beyond simple multi-cycle exception states
chapters.summary: Once multiple instructions execute concurrently and functional units have different latencies, simply waiting for each instruction to finish before fetching the next is no longer viable. Making all operations take worst-case latency would preserve order but destroys performance, motivating structures such as reorder buffers, history buffers, future files, and checkpointing.

chapters.title: Concept of the reorder buffer for in-order retirement
chapters.summary: A reorder buffer lets instructions complete out of order into a temporary hardware structure, but updates the register file or memory only when the instruction becomes the oldest and is safe to retire. Entries are allocated in program order at decode, and the buffer uses oldest and youngest pointers like a circular queue.

chapters.title: Break announcement
chapters.summary: The instructor pauses for a short break and asks students to return when the bell rings, noting that the next segment will explain reorder buffer operation in detail.

chapters.title: Reorder buffer entry fields and retirement finite-state machine
chapters.summary: The lecture enumerates the information stored in each reorder buffer entry: validity, destination register ID and value, store address and data, program counter, exception bit/type, and readiness bits. A small control machine checks the head of the ROB and, if ready and exception-free, moves the result to architectural state and advances the oldest pointer.

chapters.title: Challenge: reading source operands whose newest values are still in the reorder buffer
chapters.summary: The instructor explains that delaying register-file updates creates a new data-supply problem: a later instruction may need a value already produced into the ROB but not yet committed to the architectural register file. Options include stalling the pipeline or reading from the ROB, which introduces the need to locate the correct producer of a register value.

chapters.title: Content-addressable lookup in the reorder buffer
chapters.summary: Random-access register files can be indexed directly by register ID, but the ROB is ordered by instruction age, not architectural register number. To find a pending value, hardware may need a content-addressable memory search over destination register IDs, plus age logic to choose the youngest older matching producer among valid ROB entries.

chapters.title: Worked example: ROB search with invalid register-file entries
chapters.summary: A step-by-step example traces multiplies and adds that read and write registers such as R3, R11, and R12. The example shows how decode marks destination registers invalid, allocates ROB entries, searches the ROB for unavailable source operands, and why multiple pending writes to the same architectural register complicate lookup and wakeup.

chapters.title: Indirection with ROB tags to avoid content-addressable register-value lookup
chapters.summary: To simplify ROB access, the register file is augmented with a tag identifying the ROB entry that will produce a register’s current pending value. If a register is invalid, later instructions read the tag rather than CAM-searching the ROB, so each architectural register name is explicitly mapped to its current producing ROB entry.

chapters.title: Worked example: register renaming using ROB tags
chapters.summary: The same multiply/add example is revisited with tags: R3 is first renamed to ROB0, later to ROB2, and subsequent consumers get the correct producing entry from the register file. The instructor explains that this links producers and consumers and that later writes to the same architectural register become independent physical definitions.

chapters.title: Real processors and elimination of false dependences
chapters.summary: The lecture connects the simplified scheme to real out-of-order processors such as Intel Pentium Pro/Pentium III, which use structures like a register alias table and pointers to physical storage. Register renaming eliminates output and anti-dependences while preserving true flow dependences, effectively giving the microarchitecture many more registers than the ISA exposes.

chapters.title: Summary of in-order pipeline with ROB, tradeoffs, readings, and closing
chapters.summary: The instructor summarizes an in-order dispatch/execution pipeline with out-of-order completion and in-order retirement through a ROB, including decode allocation, execution writeback to ROB, retirement checks, exception flushing, and tag matching. The lecture closes with advantages, disadvantages, alternative precise-state mechanisms, recommended papers, and a final invitation for questions before the break.

chapters.title: Announcements and guest lecturer introduction after Easter break
chapters.summary: The lecture resumes after the Easter break and previews a return to precise exceptions and out-of-order execution. The guest lecturer, Rahul, introduces his background in microarchitecture, memory systems, data-driven microarchitecture, and mentions readings, internship/full-time opportunities, and upcoming branch prediction material.

chapters.title: Review of precise exceptions, reorder buffers, and register renaming
chapters.summary: The lecture reviews the previous in-order-dispatch pipeline with out-of-order completion and a reorder buffer (ROB) to enforce precise exceptions. It revisits flow, anti, and output dependences and explains how register renaming through ROB entries removes false dependences while preserving in-order commit.

chapters.title: Problem: in-order dispatch stalls behind unavailable operands
chapters.summary: The lecturer identifies the key limitation of the previous design: if an instruction cannot dispatch because its operands are not ready, all later instructions stall even if independent. Examples compare dependent integer multiply and load instructions, emphasizing deterministic functional-unit latency versus variable memory latency.

chapters.title: Motivation for out-of-order dispatch and dataflow execution
chapters.summary: The obvious solution is to dispatch instructions out of order when their operands are ready. The lecture connects this to dataflow execution: the program still appears as a sequential von Neumann machine, but internally instructions execute according to operand availability.

chapters.title: Alternatives to out-of-order execution: compiler scheduling, value prediction, and fine-grained multithreading
chapters.summary: The lecturer discusses other ways to tolerate dependencies: compiler scheduling can separate producers and consumers when latency is predictable, value prediction speculates producer results, and fine-grained multithreading switches among threads to cover stalls. Each approach has drawbacks, motivating why out-of-order execution became dominant.

chapters.title: Key idea of out-of-order execution: reservation stations
chapters.summary: Non-ready instructions are moved out of the way into reservation stations or instruction queues, allowing independent ready instructions to proceed to functional units. The machine fetches in program order but schedules execution in dataflow order, gaining latency tolerance.

chapters.title: Timing example: out-of-order dispatch speedup over in-order dispatch
chapters.summary: A pipeline timing diagram compares an in-order-dispatch machine with an out-of-order-dispatch machine on a short instruction sequence. Out-of-order dispatch allows independent adds to execute while a dependent instruction waits, reducing the example from 16 to 12 cycles, about a 25% speedup.

chapters.title: Q&A: register renaming, ROB necessity, and forwarding versus writeback
chapters.summary: Students ask why later instructions can use registers that earlier instructions overwrite, whether the ROB is needed in the example, and whether consumers wait for writeback. The answers clarify that renaming eliminates anti/output dependences, the ROB is needed for precise exceptions, and forwarding/bypassing can provide values before architectural writeback.

chapters.title: Four requirements for correct out-of-order execution
chapters.summary: The lecture lists the necessary mechanisms: link consumers to producers using tags, buffer waiting instructions, track source-operand readiness, and select ready instructions for dispatch to functional units. It also notes that wake-up and selection policy can be sophisticated and performance-critical.

chapters.title: Tomasulo’s algorithm and the scheduler-centered pipeline
chapters.summary: Tomasulo’s algorithm is introduced as the classic out-of-order execution method from the IBM System/360 Model 91, originally without precise exceptions. The pipeline is redrawn with an in-order front end, an out-of-order scheduler/reservation-station region, and an in-order commit side using the ROB for precise state.

chapters.title: Mechanics of Tomasulo’s algorithm: rename, wait, broadcast, and wake up
chapters.summary: The algorithm is described step by step: allocate a reservation station during renaming, copy ready operands or tags for unavailable operands, listen on the common data bus, capture matching values, wake instructions when all operands are ready, and broadcast results after execution. The lecturer begins setting up a cycle-by-cycle example before the break.

chapters.title: Break
chapters.summary: The class takes a short break and then reconvenes to continue the Tomasulo execution example.

chapters.title: Setup for cycle-by-cycle Tomasulo simulation
chapters.summary: After the break, the lecturer defines the example instruction sequence, a four-stage pipeline, pipelined add and multiply units, separate reservation stations, and an initial register alias table with all values valid. The first instructions are fetched, decoded, renamed, and inserted into reservation stations.

chapters.title: Tomasulo simulation: independent instructions issue out of order
chapters.summary: The example proceeds through cycles 4–7, showing that independent add instructions can issue while an earlier dependent add waits for a multiply result. The lecturer also explains how a later instruction that reads and writes R5 first captures the old producer tag and then renames R5 to its own new tag.

chapters.title: Tomasulo simulation: common data bus broadcasts, wake-up, and final result
chapters.summary: Cycles 8 onward show completed functional units broadcasting both tag and value over the common data bus. Matching entries in the register alias table and all reservation-station operands capture the values, dependent instructions wake up, and the sequence eventually computes the final R5 value.

chapters.title: Hardware costs and design questions for reservation stations
chapters.summary: The lecture summarizes the hardware needed for tag broadcast, value capture, wake-up, and selection: wires, comparators, and logic. It highlights the wake-up/select path as a critical timing and power cost, discusses reconstructing a data-dependence graph from a snapshot, and raises design choices such as centralized versus distributed reservation stations and deallocation timing.

chapters.title: Adding precise exceptions to out-of-order execution with a ROB
chapters.summary: To combine out-of-order execution with precise exceptions, the design reintroduces the reorder buffer to commit results in program order. The lecturer distinguishes a speculative front-end register file or RAT from a committed architectural/back-end register file, allowing recovery by discarding speculative state and restoring committed state.

chapters.title: Physical register file optimization and wrap-up
chapters.summary: The final optimization replaces repeated storage of full 64-bit values in multiple structures with pointers into a physical register file. This reduces storage by keeping values in one place while the RAT, ROB, and architectural state hold physical-register identifiers; the lecture closes by previewing superscalar execution for the next class.

chapters.title: Administrative introduction and lecture roadmap
chapters.summary: The lecture begins with a sound check, the plan to finish out-of-order execution, and previews of dataflow, superscalar execution, and branch prediction. The instructor also points to readings on combining branch predictors and superscalar microarchitecture.

chapters.title: Recap of mechanisms for out-of-order execution
chapters.summary: Reviews the four main ingredients of out-of-order execution: register renaming to link producers and consumers, reservation stations to buffer instructions, tag broadcast for readiness, and wakeup/select logic to dispatch ready instructions. The instructor emphasizes that the processor preserves the programmer’s von Neumann illusion while internally executing in dataflow order within an instruction window.

chapters.title: Precise exceptions with reorder buffers and physical register files
chapters.summary: Revisits how out-of-order processors support precise exceptions using a speculative front-end register map, an architectural register map, a reorder buffer, and a physical register file. The main idea is to store values once in the physical register file and have the rename table, architectural map, and ROB point to physical registers by tags rather than duplicating values.

chapters.title: Examples of real out-of-order processors
chapters.summary: Shows functional block diagrams of historical and modern processors using out-of-order execution, including Pentium Pro, Alpha 21264, MIPS designs, IBM POWER4, AMD Zen 2, and Apple M1. The lecture highlights rename tables, integer and floating-point physical register files, execution units, ROB size, and how ARM’s simpler ISA helps wide front ends compared with x86-64.

chapters.title: Why out-of-order execution improves latency tolerance
chapters.summary: Explains that out-of-order execution is valuable because it tolerates long-latency operations such as floating-point and memory accesses by letting independent instructions proceed. The instructor connects this to the memory wall and explains how ROB size and fetch width determine how many cycles of latency can be hidden before the instruction window fills.

chapters.title: Advantages, costs, and performance equation for out-of-order execution
chapters.summary: Summarizes benefits of out-of-order execution, especially dynamic exploitation of irregular parallelism, and its costs in complexity, critical-path delay, area, and clock-cycle time. The instructor introduces the execution-time model based on instruction count, CPI, and cycle time, and notes that out-of-order load/store execution is especially complex.

chapters.title: Survey of other ways to extract parallelism
chapters.summary: Transitions from out-of-order execution to other parallelism techniques: pipelining, fine-grained multithreading, dataflow, superscalar execution, VLIW, SIMD, and systolic arrays. The instructor frames out-of-order execution as only one method for exploiting instruction-level parallelism.

chapters.title: Definition of dataflow architecture
chapters.summary: Introduces dataflow architecture as exposing the same dependence-driven execution model that out-of-order processors build internally, but at the ISA or programming level. A dataflow node fires when its input data are ready, so data availability rather than program-counter order determines execution.

chapters.title: Why ISA-level dataflow struggled historically
chapters.summary: Explains that dataflow architectures were explored repeatedly from the 1970s through the 2000s but saw limited general-purpose adoption because they require programmers and software stacks to express programs as dataflow graphs. The instructor contrasts this with out-of-order hardware, which succeeds partly because it preserves existing sequential software while exploiting dataflow internally; FPGA kernels are mentioned as a more successful niche use.

chapters.title: Advantages and disadvantages of dataflow architectures
chapters.summary: Lists dataflow’s strengths in exploiting irregular parallelism and using only true dependences as constraints, then focuses on disadvantages: loss of precise state semantics, difficulty handling interrupts and exceptions, excessive ready parallelism, scheduling complexity, and mutable shared data structures. The lecture compares these problems to multithreaded programming without locks or barriers.

chapters.title: Definition of N-wide superscalar execution
chapters.summary: Introduces superscalar execution as widening the pipeline so multiple instructions can be fetched, decoded, renamed, executed, and retired each cycle. An N-wide superscalar processor has the hardware bandwidth to process up to N instructions per cycle, but must check dependences both across cycles and within each same-cycle fetch/decode group.

chapters.title: Superscalar design space and in-order superscalar example
chapters.summary: Clarifies that superscalar execution is independent of out-of-order execution: processors can be scalar or superscalar, and in-order or out-of-order. A two-wide in-order superscalar example shows how intra-group true dependences reduce IPC and how compiler instruction scheduling can reorder independent instructions to restore throughput while preserving correctness.

chapters.title: Superscalar benefits, costs, history, and commit bubbles
chapters.summary: Discusses superscalar advantages such as higher throughput and lower CPI, along with costs: more hardware, dependency-checking latency, complex register renaming, and possible clock-cycle increases. Historical examples include Intel Pentium as in-order superscalar, Pentium Pro as out-of-order superscalar, Alpha 21164 and 21264, and modern AMD Zen and Apple M-series widths; a Q&A explains why in-order commit from the ROB can create commit bubbles even in an 8-wide machine.

chapters.title: Break and transition to branch prediction
chapters.summary: The instructor answers a question about commit bubbles, announces a short break until 3:15, and then resumes with the second part of the lecture on branch prediction. This administrative segment separates the out-of-order/superscalar material from the control-dependence discussion.

chapters.title: Branch prediction as the next-PC problem
chapters.summary: Introduces branch prediction as the mechanism needed to keep pipelined, out-of-order, and superscalar processors fed with the correct dynamic instruction stream. The central question is what instruction address should be fetched next, especially in the presence of branches and control dependences.

chapters.title: Next-PC calculation in fixed-length versus variable-length ISAs
chapters.summary: Explains why sequential next-PC calculation is simple for fixed-length ISAs such as ARM or RISC-V, where the next instruction is usually PC + 4, but harder for variable-length ISAs such as x86, where instruction length is known only after decoding. This helps explain why fixed-length RISC ISAs can support wider front ends more easily than complex x86-style ISAs, despite x86’s code-density advantages.

chapters.title: Types of branches and their prediction difficulty
chapters.summary: Classifies control-flow instructions into conditional branches, unconditional jumps, calls, returns, and indirect branches. Conditional branches are hard because their direction is unknown at fetch time, while indirect branches are hard because their target can be one of many run-time addresses; returns are easier because a return-address stack can track call nesting.

chapters.title: Possible ways to handle control dependences
chapters.summary: Surveys alternatives for handling control dependences: stall the pipeline, predict the next fetch address, use branch delay slots, use fine-grained multithreading, eliminate branches with predication, or execute multiple paths. The instructor notes that multipath execution grows exponentially with unresolved branches, making prediction the dominant practical solution.

chapters.title: Why stalling on branches is too expensive
chapters.summary: Uses a pipeline timing example to show that waiting until decode or execute to know the next fetch address inserts bubbles and can quickly halve IPC. The lecture then sets up the quantitative motivation for branch prediction by noting that control-flow instructions are common, often around one in every five instructions.

chapters.title: Quantitative cost of branch misprediction in a wide pipeline
chapters.summary: Analyzes a 20-stage, 5-wide pipeline where every fifth instruction is a branch, showing that even 99% branch prediction accuracy can drop useful fetch IPC from 5 to about 4 and cause 20% extra wrong-path fetch work. At 90% accuracy, most cycles can be wasted on wrong paths, illustrating why modern predictors must be extremely accurate.

chapters.title: Basic always-not-taken or PC-plus-four prediction
chapters.summary: Introduces the simplest next-fetch predictor: always fetch the sequential instruction, modeled as PC + 4 for fixed-width instructions. This is a valid form of branch prediction, but it fails whenever a branch is taken, and it is even less straightforward for variable-length ISAs where PC + instruction length must be known.

chapters.title: Software layout for better fall-through prediction
chapters.summary: Shows how compilers can cooperate with simple branch prediction by arranging code so the more frequently executed path is the fall-through path in memory. The instructor mentions profile-guided code positioning and Intel trace cache as software and hardware techniques that try to make likely paths appear sequential.

chapters.title: Eliminating branches with predicate combination and predicated execution
chapters.summary: Explains two ways to reduce control-flow instructions: combine multiple conditions into one branch, or convert short if-else control dependences into data dependences using conditional expressions or predicated execution. The instructor notes that ternary or conditional operators can map differently from explicit if-else branches in hardware.

chapters.title: CPI model for naive branch prediction and preview of dynamic predictors
chapters.summary: Performs a simple CPI analysis for an always-PC-plus-four predictor: with 20% control-flow instructions, 70% taken branches, and a two-cycle wrong-path penalty, CPI rises from 1 to 1.28. The lecture concludes by identifying the two goals of branch prediction—lower the probability of a wrong guess and lower the penalty—and previews static predictors, dynamic predictors, and perceptron-based machine-learning predictors for the next lecture.

chapters.title: Announcements and setup for branch prediction lecture
chapters.summary: The lecture opens with logistics about the previous guest lecture, optional readings, homework-style reverse-engineering exercises for out-of-order execution, and optional material on load/store handling. The instructor frames branch prediction as the last major classical microarchitecture topic before VLIW, systolic arrays, and memory hierarchy.

chapters.title: Motivation: branch misprediction cost in wide deep pipelines
chapters.summary: A 20-stage, 5-wide superscalar pipeline example shows how even modest branch misprediction rates drastically reduce IPC and cause large amounts of wrong-path instruction fetch. The instructor reviews basic next-PC prediction, flushing on misprediction, fixed versus variable instruction length ISAs, compiler code layout, and trace caches.

chapters.title: Branch target buffer and front-end prediction components
chapters.summary: The lecture defines the three things needed at fetch: whether an instruction is a branch, the branch direction, and the taken target address. Direct branch targets are cached in a branch target buffer or branch target address cache, and this is combined with a direction predictor to choose between the BTB target and the next sequential PC.

chapters.title: Static branch prediction: always-not-taken, always-taken, and BTFNT
chapters.summary: Static compile-time schemes are introduced, beginning with always-not-taken and always-taken prediction. The lecture then explains the backward-taken, forward-not-taken heuristic, motivated by loop branches usually being backward and usually taken.

chapters.title: Profile-based static branch prediction and representativeness limits
chapters.summary: Profile-based prediction uses training runs to set a per-branch hint bit indicating the likely direction. Its advantage is per-branch specialization, but its accuracy depends heavily on whether the profile input set represents real runtime behavior, and it cannot model branches whose direction changes dynamically.

chapters.title: Programmer and program-analysis based static prediction
chapters.summary: The instructor describes static prediction based on compiler program analysis heuristics, such as predicting error checks as not taken, loop guards as taken, and pointer or floating-point equality comparisons as not equal. Programmer-supplied branch likelihood pragmas such as likely and unlikely are also discussed, along with OpenMP pragmas as an example of communicating source-level information to the compiler and hardware.

chapters.title: Limits of static prediction and role of dynamic compilation
chapters.summary: Static mechanisms can be combined, but all choose only one preferred direction for a branch and cannot cheaply adapt to fine-grained changes such as alternating taken/not-taken behavior. Dynamic compilation and JIT systems can recompile hot paths at runtime, but this has overhead and is not sufficient for every branch behavior pattern.

chapters.title: Dynamic branch prediction and the last-time predictor
chapters.summary: Dynamic prediction uses runtime hardware state rather than static profiles, eliminating the profile representativeness problem at the cost of extra hardware. The simplest scheme, the last-time predictor, stores one bit per branch and predicts that the next outcome will match the previous outcome, working well for long phases but failing on frequent direction changes.

chapters.title: Two-bit saturating counters and hysteresis
chapters.summary: The lecture explains why one-bit predictors change their minds too quickly and introduces hysteresis through two-bit saturating counters. Strongly and weakly taken/not-taken states improve loop prediction by mispredicting only the loop exit rather than both exit and re-entry for typical loops.

chapters.title: Why simple predictors are not enough
chapters.summary: Although two-bit predictors reached around 85–90% accuracy on many workloads and were rapidly adopted, wide and deep out-of-order processors still lose large amounts of IPC at those accuracies. The instructor introduces the two key 1991 insights: exploiting global correlation between different branches and local correlation within longer histories of the same branch.

chapters.title: Break and restart
chapters.summary: The class takes a short break and then resumes with the more advanced global and local correlation mechanisms used in real processors.

chapters.title: Global branch correlation with GHR and pattern history table
chapters.summary: Global prediction exploits the fact that the outcomes of recently executed branches and the execution path can predict the next branch. A global history register records recent taken/not-taken outcomes and indexes a pattern history table of saturating counters, forming a two-level global branch predictor.

chapters.title: Pentium Pro global predictor and Gshare hashing
chapters.summary: The Intel Pentium Pro is described as an early commercially successful out-of-order processor using a two-level global predictor with a small global history and multiple pattern history tables selected partly by branch address bits. Gshare improves global prediction by hashing the global history with the branch PC, often by XOR, to add context and reduce destructive interference.

chapters.title: Local history prediction for per-branch patterns
chapters.summary: Local prediction tracks the recent outcomes of each branch separately, enabling recognition of recurring per-branch patterns such as taken, taken, taken, not taken in short loops. The implementation uses a table of local history registers indexed by PC, followed by a pattern history table of saturating counters.

chapters.title: Design space of two-level predictors
chapters.summary: The instructor generalizes two-level prediction by varying whether the branch history register is global, per set, or per branch, and whether pattern history tables are global, per set, or per branch. This creates a large design space with different cost, latency, and aliasing tradeoffs.

chapters.title: Hybrid predictors and the Alpha 21264 tournament predictor
chapters.summary: Because different branches are best predicted by different mechanisms, hybrid predictors combine multiple algorithms and use a meta-predictor or choice predictor to select among them. The Alpha 21264 tournament predictor is presented with local and global predictors plus a chooser, improving accuracy but increasing latency, area, and complexity.

chapters.title: Biased branches, loop predictors, and remaining hard workloads
chapters.summary: The lecture explains branch filtering: simple biased branches should be identified and handled by cheap predictors so they do not pollute more sophisticated predictor tables. It then motivates advanced mechanisms for difficult workloads such as compilers, including loop predictors, perceptrons, and TAGE-style predictors with varying history lengths.

chapters.title: Perceptron branch prediction as machine learning in hardware
chapters.summary: Perceptron predictors use a simple linear classifier: global history bits are encoded as +1 or -1, multiplied by learned weights associated with a branch, and summed to predict taken or not taken. They can exploit long histories and improve accuracy, but require dot-product hardware, adder trees, training, and cannot learn linearly inseparable functions such as XOR without more complex models.

chapters.title: TAGE and predictors with multiple geometric history lengths
chapters.summary: TAGE-style predictors use multiple pattern history tables indexed with different global history lengths, ranging from short to very long, so each branch can be allocated to the history length that best predicts it. This gives many benefits of long-history prediction with less computation than perceptrons, but requires careful table sizing, hashing, tagging, and update policies.

chapters.title: State-of-the-art hybrids and branch confidence estimation
chapters.summary: Modern published predictors combine global, local, TAGE, statistical correction, loop prediction, confidence estimation, and sometimes neural-network components for very hard branches. Confidence estimation predicts whether a branch prediction is likely correct, enabling decisions such as predictor selection, speculation control, pipeline gating, energy saving, or switching threads; the lecture ends by pointing students to branch prediction competitions.

chapters.title: Announcements and roadmap for execution paradigms
chapters.summary: The lecture opens with comments on sparse attendance, possible exam coverage, and a roadmap for moving beyond superscalar execution. The instructor frames VLIW and systolic arrays as additional ways to extract concurrency, with SIMD and GPUs to follow next week.

chapters.title: Recap of superscalar execution and hardware dependence checking
chapters.summary: Superscalar processors fetch, decode, dispatch, execute, and retire multiple instructions per cycle, but require hardware to detect dependencies among concurrently fetched instructions. The instructor reviews how dependency checking trees and dispatch constraints affect IPC in a two-way superscalar example.

chapters.title: Compiler reordering to improve superscalar IPC
chapters.summary: The lecture recalls that an intelligent compiler or programmer can reorder independent instructions to improve superscalar issue efficiency. Memory dependencies, pointer chasing, branches, and unknown addresses make static dependence analysis difficult.

chapters.title: Definition of VLIW as compiler-packed instruction bundles
chapters.summary: VLIW is introduced in contrast to superscalar execution: the compiler packs independent operations into a large bundle, and hardware executes them concurrently without checking dependencies. This shifts complexity from hardware to software, aiming for simpler, faster, lower-power hardware.

chapters.title: Q&A on malicious compilers and VLIW security assumptions
chapters.summary: A student asks whether VLIW is vulnerable to a malicious compiler that packs dependent operations incorrectly. The instructor responds that the model assumes a trusted compiler and that protecting against malicious code is outside the scope of these conventional architectures.

chapters.title: VLIW program counter, operation slots, and direct routing to functional units
chapters.summary: A single program counter in VLIW names a bundle containing multiple operations, each placed in a slot corresponding to a particular processing element or functional unit. The compiler aligns operations such as multiply or add to the correct lane, reducing routing and interconnect complexity compared with superscalar machines.

chapters.title: Traditional VLIW characteristics: independent operations and lockstep bundles
chapters.summary: VLIW instructions contain multiple independent operations that can be unrelated, unlike SIMD where many lanes usually perform the same operation. Traditional VLIW machines fetch and execute multiple operations in lockstep, with fixed slot placement and statically predictable latencies.

chapters.title: Example of two-wide VLIW execution and no-op insertion
chapters.summary: A two-wide VLIW example shows how the compiler forms bundles whose operations can execute in parallel, yielding IPC 2 when independent instructions are found. When the compiler cannot find enough parallelism, it inserts no-ops, wasting issue slots and increasing pressure on compiler optimization.

chapters.title: Lockstep execution and the problem of variable-latency memory operations
chapters.summary: In pure VLIW, if one operation in a bundle stalls, all operations in that bundle stall, even if they are independent. Cache misses and other variable-latency memory operations are hard for the compiler to predict, limiting VLIW’s ability to tolerate latency compared with out-of-order execution.

chapters.title: Historical philosophy of VLIW and RISC: smart compiler, dumb machine
chapters.summary: The instructor connects VLIW to the 1970s RISC movement, where hardware was expensive and designers sought simple instructions, simple hardware, and more compiler responsibility. John Cocke’s IBM 801 work is used as an example of pushing compiler control close to hardware control signals.

chapters.title: Commercial VLIW machines and domains where VLIW succeeded
chapters.summary: The lecture cites early commercial VLIW machines and the Fisher paper’s emphasis on tightly coupled independent operations with predictable latencies. VLIW was most successful in embedded systems, DSPs, and some GPU designs, where code and memory behavior are more predictable.

chapters.title: Case study: Intel IA-64 Itanium and EPIC as VLIW-inspired ISA design
chapters.summary: Intel’s IA-64 Itanium is presented as an ambitious attempt to replace x86 during the transition to 64-bit computing with an explicitly parallel instruction computing model. Itanium used VLIW-like bundles with compiler-exposed dependence information, but adoption failed because of software migration difficulty, weak x86 binary translation, and AMD’s more compatible x86-64 path.

chapters.title: VLIW trade-offs: simple hardware versus compiler complexity and compatibility
chapters.summary: The instructor summarizes VLIW’s benefits: no dynamic scheduling, no register renaming, no dependence checking, and simpler instruction distribution after fetch. The disadvantages include hard compiler scheduling, no-op code bloat, lockstep stalls, and schedules tied closely to a particular microarchitecture generation.

chapters.title: VLIW legacy in optimizing compilers and superscalar performance
chapters.summary: Although pure VLIW has drawbacks, it drove major compiler innovations for finding many independent operations per cycle. Those optimizations now benefit ordinary superscalar processors as well, because better instruction layout and scheduling improve hardware issue efficiency.

chapters.title: Trace scheduling for hot paths across basic blocks
chapters.summary: Trace scheduling identifies frequently executed paths through a control-flow graph using profiling, then treats those basic blocks as a larger region for aggressive reordering. If execution exits the predicted trace, the compiler inserts compensation or patch-up code to preserve correctness, trading code size for parallelism.

chapters.title: Superblocks and tail duplication to eliminate side entrances
chapters.summary: Superblocks improve on traces by forming single-entry, multiple-exit regions, which enable more aggressive compiler optimizations. Tail duplication removes side entrances into a trace by copying later basic blocks so that optimized regions cannot be entered in the middle.

chapters.title: Example: superblock optimization enables strength reduction
chapters.summary: A three-operation example shows how duplicating a multiply on the rare branch path frees the hot superblock for optimization. The compiler can then recognize a common subexpression and replace a repeated multiply with a move, an example of strength reduction.

chapters.title: Predicate execution and advanced VLIW compiler issues
chapters.summary: The instructor briefly notes that predicate execution can convert control-flow dependences into data-flow dependences, helping with difficult branches. Other VLIW compiler challenges include memory bank disambiguation and static instruction scheduling for multiple-issue processors.

chapters.title: ISA translation and Transmeta Crusoe’s x86-to-VLIW code morphing
chapters.summary: ISA translation is revisited as a way to map a virtual or complex ISA onto a simpler implementation ISA. Transmeta Crusoe used code morphing software to translate and optimize x86 binaries into a proprietary VLIW ISA, achieving energy efficiency but not enough performance to beat hardware x86 implementations.

chapters.title: Dynamic code optimization as hardware–software co-design
chapters.summary: The lecture connects Transmeta-style dynamic translation to modern systems that translate x86 to ARM or optimize code at runtime with hardware support. Dynamic code optimization can also be updated in the field to fix functionality, performance, or security issues.

chapters.title: Break before systolic arrays
chapters.summary: The first part of the lecture concludes and the class takes a short break before switching from VLIW to systolic arrays.

chapters.title: Administrative note: research opportunities and architecture courses
chapters.summary: After the break, the instructor describes research opportunities for undergraduates and recommends seminar and advanced computer architecture courses. Topics mentioned include memory systems, hardware security, GPUs, TPUs, FPGAs, processing-in-memory, heterogeneous systems, health, genomics, and machine learning.

chapters.title: Motivation and modern relevance of systolic arrays
chapters.summary: Systolic arrays are introduced as a fundamental idea that became widely visible through Google’s Tensor Processing Units around 2015–2017. The instructor emphasizes that fundamental ideas may matter long before they become commercially popular.

chapters.title: Definition of systolic computation as a special-purpose execution model
chapters.summary: Systolic arrays are positioned on the special-purpose side of the architecture spectrum: they trade generality for efficiency and performance. They implement systolic computation, originally used for convolution, filtering, pattern matching, matrix-vector computation, image processing, signal processing, and robotics, and now central to machine learning acceleration.

chapters.title: Systolic array motivation: balancing computation with I/O bandwidth
chapters.summary: The goal is to replace a single processing element with a regular array and carefully orchestrate data movement so that data read once from memory is transformed by many processing elements before returning to memory. This improves data reuse, concurrency, and the balance between computation and memory bandwidth.

chapters.title: Linear systolic array analogy: memory as heart and data as blood
chapters.summary: A linear chain of processing elements illustrates how data is pumped rhythmically through cells, with each cell performing part of the computation and passing data along. The term systolic comes from the analogy to blood pulsing from the heart through cells and back.

chapters.title: Why systolic arrays are more general than simple pipelines
chapters.summary: Although a linear systolic array resembles a pipeline, systolic arrays can be multidimensional, have multidirectional connections, and contain local memories or kernels inside processing elements. Unlike an instruction pipeline, the processing elements are not fixed fetch/decode/execute stages but computation units for an application-specific dataflow.

chapters.title: Convolution as a target computation for systolic acceleration
chapters.summary: Convolution is introduced as a computation used in filtering, pattern matching, image processing, statistics, and convolutional neural networks. The instructor explains one-dimensional and two-dimensional convolution as applying weights or kernels to input data to produce output feature maps.

chapters.title: Expressing convolution as matrix multiplication and the AlexNet GPU story
chapters.summary: The instructor shows that convolution can be rearranged into matrix multiplication, explaining why GPUs and systolic hardware can accelerate convolutional neural networks. A historical aside describes AlexNet, Jeff Hinton’s group, and GPU-based training that helped trigger modern deep learning progress.

chapters.title: One-dimensional systolic hardware for convolution
chapters.summary: A specialized linear systolic array for convolution is described, where each processing element stores a stationary weight, passes input values to the right, and sends accumulated outputs to the left. Each PE performs multiply-accumulate, computing terms such as y = y + w × x as values arrive at carefully timed cycles.

chapters.title: Design issues in specialized systolic convolution arrays
chapters.summary: The lecture notes that multiply and add units can be organized to overlap operations, and that the essential difficulty is orchestrating when inputs enter the array and when outputs are captured. Higher-dimensional arrays or unpredictable PE latencies make timing and buffering more complex.

chapters.title: Two-dimensional systolic array for matrix multiplication
chapters.summary: A 3×3 matrix multiplication example shows a 2D systolic array of nine processing elements, each accumulating one output element. Matrix elements from A and B enter from different directions and move across the array so that each PE performs the necessary multiply-accumulate operations over several cycles.

chapters.title: Other systolic arrays and specialized numerical computations
chapters.summary: The instructor mentions that systolic arrays can be designed for many computations beyond convolution and matrix multiplication, including least-squares fitting, orthogonal triangularization, and triangular-system solving. These designs use carefully timed data inputs, delay elements, and chained arrays rather than general-purpose instruction streams.

chapters.title: Advantages and disadvantages of systolic arrays
chapters.summary: Systolic arrays are highly efficient when the computation fits the processing-element functions and organization, because they exploit regularity, concurrency, and data reuse with limited memory bandwidth. Their weakness is specialization: irregular or mismatched computations may be inefficient, difficult, or impossible to map.

chapters.title: Generalizing systolic computation into stream and pipeline parallelism
chapters.summary: The instructor explains how adding small memories, selectable weights, or instruction and data memory to each processing element makes systolic arrays more programmable. This leads to generalized systolic computation, stream processing, and pipeline parallelism where different stages of a program run on different cores or specialized units.

chapters.title: History: H. T. Kung’s Warp computer at Carnegie Mellon
chapters.summary: H. T. Kung’s Warp computer is presented as an early systolic-array accelerator built at CMU for vision and robotics workloads. It used a linear array of processing cells, a host machine, a high-level language, and an optimizing compiler, anticipating many ideas later used in accelerator programming.

chapters.title: Google TPU systolic matrix multiplication unit
chapters.summary: Google’s TPU is described as using a large systolic matrix multiplication unit to reduce reads and writes to the unified buffer and save energy. Data and weights are fed through the array under compiler control, with system-level support for offloading matrix multiplication from higher-level software.

chapters.title: Scaling TPUs with high-bandwidth memory, interconnects, and VLIW sequencing
chapters.summary: Later TPU generations add high-bandwidth memory, floating-point support, and interconnects so that many TPUs can work together on larger models. The instructor notes that TPUs combine paradigms, including VLIW-like core sequencers for irregular control work alongside systolic arrays for dense matrix computation.

chapters.title: Memory bottlenecks in systolic accelerators and closing comparison to other ML hardware
chapters.summary: The lecture concludes by noting that even powerful systolic arrays can become bottlenecked by data movement through DRAM and interconnects, with some large models spending most energy outside computation. The instructor contrasts systolic arrays with SIMD-based wafer-scale engines and FPGA accelerators, then previews SIMD and GPU coverage next week.

chapters.title: Introduction to SIMD architectures and course logistics
chapters.summary: The lecture introduces single instruction, multiple data architectures as a foundation for GPUs and machine-learning accelerators. It also mentions optional material on decoupled access/execute architectures, readings, and the connection to accelerators such as Google TPU systolic arrays.

chapters.title: Flynn’s taxonomy and the role of SIMD
chapters.summary: SIMD is presented as a way to exploit regular data-level parallelism, such as element-wise array addition. Flynn’s taxonomy is reviewed: SISD, SIMD, MISD, and MIMD, with modern systems described as combinations of these paradigms.

chapters.title: Definition of data parallelism and comparison with other parallelism
chapters.summary: Data parallelism is defined as performing the same operation on many data elements, with examples including vector addition, dot product, and matrix multiplication. The lecturer contrasts it with dataflow parallelism, thread/control parallelism, and general instruction-level parallelism, noting that reductions introduce serial dependencies.

chapters.title: Time-space duality: array processors versus vector processors
chapters.summary: The lecture distinguishes array processors, which apply one instruction to many data elements simultaneously using multiple processing elements, from vector processors, which pipeline operations across consecutive cycles. Vector registers are introduced as registers that hold multiple data elements rather than one scalar value.

chapters.title: Example: executing load-add-multiply-store on array and vector processors
chapters.summary: A four-element vector code sequence is used to compare execution on an array processor and a vector processor. Array processors perform the same operation across elements in parallel, while vector processors overlap different stages of the loop in a pipeline and reach high throughput at steady state.

chapters.title: SIMD versus VLIW and basic vector-processor requirements
chapters.summary: SIMD is compared with VLIW: SIMD amortizes instruction fetch and decode overhead by applying one instruction to many data elements, whereas VLIW packs independent operations into a long instruction. The lecture then defines vectors, vector length, vector stride, and explains stride using row-major matrix multiplication.

chapters.title: Why vector instructions allow deep pipelines
chapters.summary: Vector processors can use deeper pipelines because elements within a vector usually have no data dependences, no control-flow branches, and predictable strided memory addresses. These properties enable higher clock frequency, prefetch-like address generation, loop elimination, and efficient pipelining for regular memory access patterns.

chapters.title: Advantages and limitations of vector processors
chapters.summary: The lecturer summarizes benefits of vector machines: no dependencies within a vector, amortized instruction overhead, implicit loop execution, and regular memory access. The main limitations are poor performance on irregular parallelism such as pointer chasing and difficulty programming data layouts to match the hardware; GPUs are previewed as improving the programming model.

chapters.title: Amdahl’s law and memory-bandwidth bottlenecks
chapters.summary: Amdahl’s law is revisited: speedup from SIMD is limited by serial portions such as reductions, motivating designs with both many small cores and powerful scalar cores. The lecture then explains that SIMD machines require high memory bandwidth, and performance can be limited by compute-memory imbalance or memory-bank conflicts.

chapters.title: Vector control registers, masks, and Cray vector machines
chapters.summary: Vector processor components are detailed: vector data registers, vector length, vector stride, vector mask registers, and pipelined vector functional units. Cray-1 and Cray X-MP are shown as historical SIMD/vector machines combining vector and scalar pipelines with many memory banks.

chapters.title: Break
chapters.summary: The lecturer pauses the lecture and asks students to return after a 15-minute break.

chapters.title: Seymour Cray’s oxen-versus-chickens question
chapters.summary: After the break, the lecturer discusses Seymour Cray’s question about whether to use a few strong processors or many small ones. This motivates the design tradeoff between powerful cores and many lightweight cores, depending on how embarrassingly parallel the workload is.

chapters.title: Memory banking for one-element-per-cycle vector loads
chapters.summary: The lecture explains why vector processors need many memory banks: if memory latency exceeds one cycle, interleaving consecutive elements across independent banks can sustain one element per cycle. The key condition is that the number of banks should cover the bank access latency, assuming stride-one accesses without conflicts.

chapters.title: Performance example: scalar loop versus vectorized loop
chapters.summary: A loop computing the average of arrays A and B into C is translated into scalar assembly, and its dynamic instruction count and execution time are computed. The loop is then vectorized using vector length and stride registers, reducing dynamic instructions and improving execution time from thousands of cycles to hundreds.

chapters.title: Vector chaining and the effect of memory ports
chapters.summary: The lecturer introduces vector chaining, analogous to forwarding, where the output of one vector functional unit can feed another before the full vector register is complete. Performance improves further when memory banks provide multiple load and store ports, allowing more overlap among loads, arithmetic, shifts, and stores.

chapters.title: Q&A: memory banks versus memory ports
chapters.summary: A student asks how memory banks and memory ports interact. The lecturer explains that ports allow more direct parallel access but are expensive and hard to scale, while banking is a more cost-efficient, scalable way to pipeline memory accesses across consecutive cycles.

chapters.title: Vector strip mining, gather/scatter, and sparse access
chapters.summary: When a data set is larger than the maximum vector-register length, the loop is broken into chunks using vector strip mining, with a shorter final vector iteration. For irregular memory layouts, gather and scatter operations use indirect indexing to pack or store non-contiguous elements, which is important for sparse vectors and sparse matrix operations.

chapters.title: Masked vector execution for conditional operations
chapters.summary: Conditional branches inside vectorized loops are handled with vector masks and predicated execution. The lecture shows how masks implement if and if-else behavior, then compares hardware implementations that either execute all operations and suppress masked writeback or only execute active mask elements.

chapters.title: Stride, bank conflicts, and memory-bank mapping
chapters.summary: The lecture revisits the condition that stride and bank count should be relatively prime to avoid conflicts and sustain one element per cycle. Matrix operations with different row and column strides complicate bank access, so mitigations include more banks, more ports, improved data layout, and pseudorandom bank mapping.

chapters.title: Combining array and vector processing with SIMD lanes
chapters.summary: Modern SIMD processors are described as hybrids that exploit parallelism in both time and space. Multiple SIMD lanes act like array-processing elements, while each lane is internally vector-like and pipelines operations over a subset of vector elements.

chapters.title: Automatic vectorization and lecture summary
chapters.summary: The lecturer discusses the difficulty of automatic compiler vectorization: simple loops can be vectorized, but complex code often remains hard for both compilers and programmers. The summary emphasizes that SIMD works best for regular data-level parallelism, is limited by vectorizability and scalar portions, and appears in many ISAs.

chapters.title: SIMD extensions in modern ISAs: MMX, SSE, and AVX
chapters.summary: The final section explains packed SIMD instructions in general-purpose ISAs, beginning with Intel MMX packed addition that partitions a register into smaller fields and suppresses carry propagation between them. Examples include packed compare, packed multiply-add, image background compositing with masks, and later extensions such as SSE and AVX.

chapters.title: Announcements: remaining lectures on memory and start of GPU architectures
chapters.summary: The lecture opens with course pacing and an announcement that the remaining lectures will focus on memory systems, the major bottleneck in current systems. The instructor introduces GPUs as the day’s topic, building on the prior SIMD, array processor, and vector processor lecture.

chapters.title: Review of SIMD, Flynn’s taxonomy, array/vector processing, and memory banking
chapters.summary: The lecture reviews data-parallel execution through Flynn’s taxonomy and the distinction between array and vector processors, emphasizing that modern SIMD machines combine space and time parallelism. It also revisits memory banking, bank conflicts, and why high-throughput memories are essential for SIMD and GPU execution.

chapters.title: Review of vector lanes, partitioned registers, vector pipelines, and automatic vectorization
chapters.summary: The instructor revisits how vector processors use multiple lanes, partitioned vector register files, and overlapped vector instructions to exploit parallelism. A simple loop example illustrates automatic code vectorization and the compiler’s challenge of proving that loop iterations are independent.

chapters.title: Vectorizable loops, graphics parallelism, Amdahl’s law, and SIMD ISA extensions
chapters.summary: A perfectly vectorizable array loop is used to explain why graphics workloads fit SIMD so well, because the same operation is applied to many pixels. The lecture connects this to Amdahl’s law and the serial bottleneck, then reviews CPU SIMD extensions such as Intel MMX, SSE, AVX, AVX-512, and AMX as examples of SIMD added to scalar ISAs.

chapters.title: Prevalence of SIMD in Cerebras wafer-scale engines and FPGA accelerators
chapters.summary: Before focusing on GPUs, the instructor discusses other SIMD-based accelerators, including the Cerebras wafer-scale engine and Microsoft FPGA-based neural network accelerators. These systems combine multiple paradigms such as MIMD, distributed memory, routers, local SRAM, and small SIMD units for machine learning workloads.

chapters.title: Class poll and motivation for GPU success in AI and interconnects
chapters.summary: The instructor asks who has programmed GPUs and notes that most students use GPUs indirectly through laptops or large language models. GPUs are motivated as successful accelerators not only because of their compute engines, but also because large AI models require fast interconnects between many GPUs.

chapters.title: GPU cores as SIMD engines with a thread-based programming model
chapters.summary: GPUs are introduced as SIMD engines underneath, but with a programming model based on scalar threads rather than explicit vector instructions. The lecture distinguishes programming models from execution models and explains that GPUs use an SPMD programming model implemented efficiently on SIMD hardware.

chapters.title: Three ways to exploit loop parallelism: sequential, SIMD, and multithreaded SPMD
chapters.summary: Using the same independent loop, the instructor compares sequential execution on pipelined, out-of-order, superscalar, and VLIW processors with explicit data-parallel SIMD execution. The discussion then transitions to a multithreaded version where each iteration becomes a scalar thread, setting up the GPU SIMT model.

chapters.title: Definition of SIMT: scalar threads dynamically grouped into SIMD-like warps
chapters.summary: The multithreaded formulation is explained as single program, multiple data: many scalar threads execute the same code on different data. NVIDIA’s SIMT terminology is introduced as a GPU execution style where scalar threads are grouped dynamically, rather than being programmed with vector instructions.

chapters.title: Thread contexts, warps, wavefronts, and dynamic grouping by program counter
chapters.summary: Each GPU thread has its own context and can in principle be scheduled independently, but hardware groups threads at the same program counter into warps or wavefronts. A warp is presented as a SIMD operation formed by hardware, allowing one fetched instruction to drive many scalar lanes.

chapters.title: Fine-grained multiwarping for simple pipelines and latency tolerance
chapters.summary: Warps are interleaved through the pipeline using fine-grained multithreading, so different pipeline stages can hold instructions from different warps. This keeps the pipeline simple by reducing needs for branch prediction and dependency checking, but requires storage for many thread contexts and register files.

chapters.title: Break
chapters.summary: The instructor pauses the lecture for a short break and invites questions before continuing.

chapters.title: Clarification: lockstep execution, control overhead amortization, active masks, and memory stalls
chapters.summary: After the break, the instructor clarifies that once threads are grouped into a warp, they execute in lockstep like a vector instruction, so one stalled thread can stall the warp. The GPU core diagram is then expanded to show warp scheduling, active masks for branches, partitioned register files, and queues for warps waiting on long-latency memory accesses.

chapters.title: Mapping vector-machine concepts to GPU warps, memory coalescing, CUDA kernels, blocks, and threads
chapters.summary: The lecture maps vector-add execution directly onto a 32-thread warp, showing that the hardware resembles a SIMD machine even though the program uses scalar thread IDs. It then explains regular memory access patterns, the need for memory bandwidth, heterogeneous CPU-GPU execution, and CUDA’s kernel, block, and thread abstractions.

chapters.title: Mapping programmer-visible blocks to warps and streaming multiprocessors
chapters.summary: GPU cores are described as SIMD pipelines, called streaming processors or streaming multiprocessors in NVIDIA terminology. Programmer-visible blocks are divided into warps, which are mapped to streaming multiprocessors, and the lecture contrasts traditional SIMD with warp-based SIMD and notes synchronization through GPU shared memory.

chapters.title: Branch divergence, active masks, SIMD utilization, and dynamic warp formation
chapters.summary: Conditional control flow causes threads in a warp to take different paths, producing branch divergence and lowering SIMD utilization because only some lanes perform useful work. The lecture explains active-mask splitting and reconvergence, then introduces dynamic warp formation as a hardware technique for regrouping threads at the same program counter to improve lane utilization.

chapters.title: GPU analysis, homework hints, warp scheduling for memory latency, and subwarping
chapters.summary: The instructor notes that GPU behavior can be analyzed with reverse-engineering-style homework questions, especially by computing SIMD utilization. The lecture then discusses scheduling policies that avoid having many warps reach long-latency cache misses simultaneously, plus subwarping and other mechanisms for improving utilization under divergence and memory stalls.

chapters.title: Evolution of NVIDIA GPUs: shader cores, Tensor Cores, sparsity support, and low-precision data types
chapters.summary: An example NVIDIA GPU lineage is used to show increasing parallelism, from many SIMD functional units and thread contexts in older GPUs to Volta Tensor Cores specialized for matrix multiplication. Later designs add sparse matrix support and low-precision formats such as FP16, bfloat16, FP8, 4-bit, and possibly 1-bit representations to raise throughput for machine learning.

chapters.title: Wrap-up: trade-offs among GPUs, systolic arrays, FPGAs, and heterogeneous systems for machine learning
chapters.summary: The lecture ends by comparing execution models for machine learning: GPU shader cores are flexible SIMD engines, Tensor Cores and systolic arrays can be more efficient for matrix multiplication, and FPGAs offer another design point. The instructor closes with resources for heterogeneous systems and GPU programming.

chapters.title: Announcements: GPU programming lecture, readings, and transition to memory
chapters.summary: The lecture opens with a brief sparsity joke, announces an optional GPU programming lecture and heterogeneous systems material, and points students to memory systems readings. The instructor frames the course transition from computation-focused execution models to memory systems and memory hierarchy.

chapters.title: Review of execution models and processing paradigm trade-offs
chapters.summary: The instructor reviews previously covered processing approaches, including out-of-order execution, decoupled access/execute, pipelining, SIMD, GPUs, FPGAs, and systolic arrays. The focus is on trade-offs among specialization, efficiency, programmability, flexibility, and hardware cost.

chapters.title: Motivation: memory and communication dominate modern systems
chapters.summary: The lecture shifts from processing to memory, storage, I/O, and communication, arguing that modern chips devote most area and resources to caches, register files, interconnects, memory interfaces, and storage-related structures. Examples include AMD Barcelona, Intel Pentium Pro, AMD Ryzen, IBM Power10, GPUs, and wafer-scale systems.

chapters.title: Claim that memory remains the system bottleneck despite dominating hardware resources
chapters.summary: Using a memory-system platform diagram, the instructor argues that most hardware real estate is devoted to memory and data movement, yet memory is still the bottleneck. The point is framed as a blank-slate design question: if more than 99% of resources are memory-related, why is memory still limiting performance?

chapters.title: Course examples where memory latency shaped processor design
chapters.summary: The instructor connects memory bottlenecks to earlier course topics: load-use delays in pipelines, load/store handling in out-of-order execution, VLIW stalls, SIMD memory banking, GPU register files, systolic arrays, and fine-grained multithreading. These mechanisms are presented as ways to tolerate or work around memory latency.

chapters.title: Application perspective: data-intensive workloads stress memory capacity, latency, and bandwidth
chapters.summary: Modern workloads such as machine learning, AI, genomics, web browsing, video processing, and mobile inference are described as increasingly data-intensive. Different applications, and even different phases of the same application, may be limited by memory latency, bandwidth, or capacity.

chapters.title: Historical performance evidence: “It’s the Memory, Stupid!” and processor stalls
chapters.summary: The instructor cites Richard Sites’s Alpha processor article “It’s the Memory, Stupid!” and PhD-era Intel workload studies showing processors operating far below peak throughput because they wait for memory. The examples show that even aggressive superscalar processors often spend most time stalled on cache misses and memory latency.

chapters.title: Google data-center evidence that processors retire instructions only a small fraction of time
chapters.summary: A Google ISCA 2015 study is used to show that large-scale data-center workloads spend much of their time backend-bound or frontend-bound, with memory playing a major role. The instructor emphasizes that cutting-edge processors may retire useful instructions only around 10–20% of the time.
