chapters.title: Energy cost of data movement versus computation
chapters.summary: The lecture compares the energy of arithmetic operations with the energy of SRAM access, DRAM access, on-chip interconnect traversal, and off-chip communication. NVIDIA data is used to argue that moving data can cost hundreds to thousands of times more energy than computation, especially for simple integer operations.

chapters.title: Q&A: relationship between energy consumption and heat
chapters.summary: A student asks whether high energy consumption directly implies heat. The instructor explains that heat depends not only on total energy but also on how quickly energy is dissipated, with high-frequency computation units typically causing intense heat, although communication also contributes.

chapters.title: Mobile and neural-network studies showing memory dominates system energy
chapters.summary: The instructor summarizes Google collaborations on mobile workloads and Pixel-phone neural network models, finding that more than 60% and sometimes more than 90% of total system energy is spent in memory and data movement. Specialized accelerators make computation more efficient, so unoptimized memory movement dominates by Amdahl’s law, motivating processing-in-memory.

chapters.title: Robustness perspective: DRAM scaling and RowHammer
chapters.summary: The instructor introduces robustness as another reason memory is critical, citing a Facebook data-center study correlating DRAM density with failure rate. RowHammer is reviewed as a DRAM disturbance effect where repeated row activations can induce bit flips in adjacent rows before refresh.

chapters.title: Mechanism and implications of RowHammer disturbance errors
chapters.summary: The lecture explains RowHammer using the abstraction of DRAM as a two-dimensional array: activating and precharging rows repeatedly perturbs neighboring cells and leaks charge from capacitors. The instructor emphasizes that ordinary loads should not architecturally modify other locations, yet RowHammer can corrupt data belonging to other applications or the operating system and has security implications.

chapters.title: Memory-centric computing as a research and startup opportunity
chapters.summary: After summarizing memory’s effects on performance, energy, robustness, cost, form factor, quality of service, predictability, and sustainability, the instructor argues for memory-centric rather than processor-centric innovation. Memory is presented as a more disruptive area for future systems research and companies.

chapters.title: Programmer view: loads, stores, and virtual memory abstraction
chapters.summary: The instructor contrasts the programmer’s simple view of memory through loads and stores with the physical reality of finite memory and banks. Virtual memory is introduced as the ISA-level abstraction in which system software and hardware translate virtual addresses to physical memory transparently.

chapters.title: Backing store and the extended storage hierarchy
chapters.summary: Virtual memory requires a larger backing store so a limited physical memory can appear larger to programs. The instructor outlines the broader hierarchy from registers and SRAM caches through DRAM main memory, SSDs, hard disks, and tape.

chapters.title: Ideal memory and conflicting design goals
chapters.summary: The lecture defines the ideal memory as having zero latency, zero cost, zero energy, infinite capacity, and infinite bandwidth. These goals conflict: larger memories tend to be slower, less robust, and more energy-consuming, motivating a hierarchy of small fast memories near the processor and larger slower memories farther away.

chapters.title: Memory technologies: flip-flops, SRAM, DRAM, flash, disks, and tape
chapters.summary: The instructor compares storage technologies by speed, density, volatility, manufacturing requirements, and cost per bit. Flip-flops are fastest but extremely expensive, SRAM is fast but costly, DRAM is dense but requires refresh and special capacitor processes, while flash, disks, and tape are slower but nonvolatile and high capacity.

chapters.title: Basic memory array organization with rows, columns, decoders, and multiplexers
chapters.summary: All memories are introduced as two-dimensional arrays of bit cells accessed through address selection logic and readout circuitry. The instructor revisits a small 4-by-3 memory example and generalizes it to larger arrays with word lines, bit lines, row decoders, column multiplexers, and limited access granularity.

chapters.title: Break and restart of memory hierarchy discussion
chapters.summary: The instructor pauses for a break and then resumes by saying the next topic is how to build a hierarchy of memory arrays. Banking is introduced as the key concept for scaling memory capacity and parallelism.

chapters.title: Definition of memory banking and interleaving
chapters.summary: Banking, also called interleaving, divides a large monolithic memory array into smaller independently accessible banks. This can reduce access latency and enable overlapping or parallel accesses, but performance depends on how addresses are mapped across banks.

chapters.title: Bus and pin trade-offs in multi-bank memory interfaces
chapters.summary: The instructor compares a design with separate address and data buses per bank to a cheaper shared-bus design. DRAM chips typically share address and data buses across banks to reduce pin count, chip cost, and off-chip wiring complexity.

chapters.title: Top-down DRAM organization: banks, chips, ranks, modules, channels, and controllers
chapters.summary: A DRAM system is built hierarchically from banks inside chips, chips combined into ranks, ranks placed on DIMM modules, and modules connected to memory channels controlled by memory controllers. Commands, addresses, and data travel over separate buses, and multiple channels add another dimension of parallelism.

chapters.title: 3D-stacked memory and high-bandwidth memory
chapters.summary: The lecture explains that modern high-performance memories are increasingly three-dimensional, stacking DRAM dies and sometimes logic dies with dense vertical interconnects. High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) and 2.5D interposer-based systems provide much higher bandwidth than planar pin-limited packages, though heat and thermals become harder.

chapters.title: DIMM, rank, chip, and bank hierarchy in a DRAM system
chapters.summary: The instructor walks through a concrete DRAM module with channels, DIMMs, ranks, chips, and banks. Ranks increase capacity and interface width by making multiple chips respond to the same command, while banks inside each chip provide parallelism behind a narrow external interface.

chapters.title: Q&A: serial presence detect on a DIMM
chapters.summary: A student asks about the small SPD structure on the memory module. The instructor explains that serial presence detect is a small nonvolatile memory used by the memory controller to identify the module and determine parameters such as supported timings.

chapters.title: Ranks and chips as synchronized responders to memory commands
chapters.summary: The instructor continues explaining ranks: all chips in a rank receive the same command and address and each supplies a slice of the data, such as 8 bits of a 64-bit transfer. Sharing buses lowers cost and pin count, but switching between ranks incurs a timing penalty.

chapters.title: DRAM bank operation with row buffers, activate, read, and precharge commands
chapters.summary: Inside a bank, a row is activated and sensed into a row buffer, after which column reads can retrieve selected data. Accesses to the open row are row-buffer hits and are much faster than row-buffer conflicts, which require precharging the current row, activating another row, and then reading the desired column.

chapters.title: Internal DRAM bank hierarchy with subarrays and mats
chapters.summary: The row-buffer abstraction is refined: real DRAM banks are too large to build as one flat array, so they are divided into smaller subarrays and mats with local sense amplifiers and global I/O. This hierarchy balances latency, robustness, capacity, bandwidth, power, cost, and reliability.

chapters.title: Sense amplifier and DRAM cell circuit operation
chapters.summary: The instructor explains the sense amplifier as a cross-coupled inverter structure that amplifies a small voltage difference to a full logic level. A DRAM cell stores charge in a capacitor; reading perturbs the bit line, the sense amplifier detects and amplifies the value, and the charge is restored because DRAM reads are destructive.

chapters.title: Subarray row-buffer cost and chip-level I/O paths
chapters.summary: A subarray uses a row of sense amplifiers as its row buffer, amortizing expensive sensing circuitry across many DRAM cells. The instructor discusses how data moves from local row buffers to global sense amplifiers and shared internal buses, and how activate, read/write, and precharge operations require long, power-hungry interconnects.

chapters.title: Mapping a 64-byte cache block onto DRAM chips and transfers
chapters.summary: The instructor shows how a 64-byte cache block can be mapped to a channel, rank, DIMM, row, and columns. With eight x8 DRAM chips, each I/O cycle returns 64 bits, so eight sequential column transfers from the row buffer deliver the full 64-byte block.

chapters.title: Comparison of DRAM and SRAM technology before moving to caches
chapters.summary: The lecture closes by contrasting DRAM’s one-transistor-one-capacitor dynamic storage with SRAM’s six-transistor cross-coupled inverter cell. The instructor notes that SRAM and DRAM banks are organized similarly at a high level, but off-chip DRAM serializes row and column addresses to reduce pins, setting up the next lecture on caches.

chapters.title: Opening announcements and lecture plan for memory hierarchy
chapters.summary: The lecture opens with a livestream check, a welcome after the holiday, and a preview: finish the memory-technology discussion, then move into memory hierarchy and cache organization. Reading material for this and the next lecture is also noted.

chapters.title: Review of ideal memory, memory arrays, SRAM, and DRAM organization
chapters.summary: The instructor reviews why memory matters for performance, energy, cost, robustness, and sustainability, and recalls the impossible ideal of zero-latency, infinite-capacity memory. The lecture recaps memory arrays, SRAM and DRAM cells, bank organization, DRAM hierarchy such as channels/ranks/banks/subarrays/mats, and read/precharge/refresh behavior.

chapters.title: Comparison of DRAM and SRAM tradeoffs
chapters.summary: DRAM is compared with SRAM: DRAM is denser and cheaper because of its 1T1C cell, but slower, destructive on reads, refresh-dependent, and hard to integrate with logic processes. SRAM is faster, does not require refresh, and is compatible with processor manufacturing, but is less dense and more expensive.

chapters.title: Introduction to phase-change memory and Intel Optane
chapters.summary: The lecture introduces emerging memory technologies, focusing on phase-change memory (PCM), where chalcogenide material switches between amorphous and crystalline phases with different resistivity and reflectivity. Examples include rewritable CDs, PCM research as DRAM replacement or hybrid DRAM-PCM memory, and Intel Optane / 3D XPoint persistent memory and SSD products.

chapters.title: DRAM versus PCM and charge versus resistive memory
chapters.summary: DRAM and PCM are compared: DRAM is faster but less dense and volatile, while PCM is denser, nonvolatile, refresh-free, but slower, higher-energy for writes, less mature to manufacture, and limited by endurance. The instructor distinguishes charge memories such as DRAM and flash from resistive memories such as PCM, STT-MRAM, and memristors.

chapters.title: Why emerging memory technologies and processing-in-memory matter
chapters.summary: The lecture explains that flash memory was once uncertain but became transformative, and notes that SSD controllers hide many flash reliability problems from the host. The instructor then motivates processing-in-memory as a complementary approach to DRAM limitations by reducing costly data movement in processor-centric von Neumann systems.

chapters.title: Motivation for memory hierarchy and quantitative device tradeoffs
chapters.summary: The lecture starts the memory-hierarchy section by explaining that no single memory can be both very fast, very large, cheap, high-bandwidth, and low-energy. Examples and tables compare registers, SRAM caches, DRAM, PCM/Optane, flash SSDs, hard disks, and tapes, showing that lower levels are generally larger, slower, cheaper per bit, and more energy-expensive to access.

chapters.title: Definition of hierarchical memory levels and cache capacities
chapters.summary: The instructor states the core idea of memory hierarchy: use multiple levels that become progressively larger and slower farther from the processor, while keeping most needed data in faster levels. Representative capacities and latencies are given for L1, L2, L3, and main memory.

chapters.title: Principle of temporal and spatial locality in programs
chapters.summary: The lecture introduces locality as the reason memory hierarchy works: recent behavior predicts near-future behavior. Temporal locality is illustrated by repeated accesses in loops and counters, while spatial locality is illustrated by arrays, vectors, stride-one accesses, and sequential instruction fetches.

chapters.title: Break and return from break
chapters.summary: The instructor stops for a short break and asks students to return at 3:15. After the break, the lecture resumes by reconnecting locality to cache design.

chapters.title: How caches exploit temporal and spatial locality
chapters.summary: Caching is defined as automatically managed fast memory that stores recently accessed data to exploit temporal locality. To exploit spatial locality, memory is divided into fixed-size cache blocks or cache lines, so fetching one byte or word brings nearby bytes as well; historical examples include Wilkes’s slave memory idea and IBM System/360 Model 85 cache blocks.

chapters.title: Pipeline integration and manual versus automatic cache management
chapters.summary: Caches must be tightly integrated into the processor pipeline, ideally with fast L1 access so loads do not stall too much; this motivates multi-level cache hierarchies. The instructor contrasts hardware-managed caches with software-managed scratchpad memories, citing embedded processors, NVIDIA GPU shared memory, GPGPU evolution, Ampere/Hopper configurable L1/shared memory, and Cerebras on-chip scratchpad memory.

chapters.title: Historical perspective on memory and modern hierarchy management
chapters.summary: The lecture briefly reviews historical memory technologies such as magnetic drum memory and magnetic core memory, then connects them to early cache ideas. A modern hierarchy is described in terms of what is managed by compiler/software versus hardware: registers are compiler-managed, L1/L2/L3 caches are usually hardware-managed, and main-memory-to-disk movement is managed by the operating system through virtual memory.

chapters.title: Derivation of cache hierarchy access-time equations and AMAT example
chapters.summary: The instructor derives recursive perceived access time for a memory level using intrinsic access time, hit rate, miss rate, and the next-level perceived access time. An Intel Pentium 4-style example with L1, L2, and DRAM latencies shows how L1 and L2 miss rates trade off, and how average latency can be improved by better hit rates or deeper/faster hierarchy levels.

chapters.title: Cache abstraction, blocks, tag store, and design decisions
chapters.summary: A cache is defined broadly as a structure that memorizes previously used or produced data to avoid repeating long-latency operations, with processor caches storing frequently or recently accessed memory blocks. The lecture introduces data stores, tag stores, valid bits, hit/miss checks, and major cache design choices: placement, replacement, block granularity, write policy, and whether instruction and data caches are separate.

chapters.title: Direct-mapped cache organization and address decomposition
chapters.summary: The lecture explains direct-mapped caches using a toy example with 256 bytes of memory, a 64-byte cache, and 8-byte blocks. Addresses are split into tag, index, and block-offset fields; the index selects one cache entry, the tag is compared to determine hit or miss, and blocks with the same index conflict because only one can reside there.

chapters.title: Set-associative and fully associative caches
chapters.summary: The instructor shows how direct-mapped caches can have 0% hit rate for interleaved conflicting blocks, motivating set associativity. In a set-associative cache, an index selects a set and multiple ways are searched in parallel; increasing associativity reduces conflict misses but increases tag comparisons and multiplexing, with fully associative caches as the extreme case.

chapters.title: Closing and next lecture preview
chapters.summary: The lecture ends by noting that the next lecture will continue with associativity tradeoffs and the challenges introduced by more associative cache designs. Students are wished a good weekend.

chapters.title: Motivation: locality, communication cost, and why caches exist
chapters.summary: The lecture resumes caching by emphasizing temporal and spatial locality as strong program properties, illustrated with classroom seating and an airline-routing anecdote. It frames caches as a way to exploit locality and reduce long-distance data movement, while noting that future systems may instead move computation closer to memory to save energy.

chapters.title: Memory hierarchy beyond one machine: local and remote memory nodes
chapters.summary: The memory hierarchy is reviewed as a way to combine small fast storage with larger slower storage. The discussion extends the hierarchy to data-center systems with compute nodes, memory blades, and remote memory accessed over low-latency networks.

chapters.title: Direct-mapped, set-associative, and fully associative caches
chapters.summary: The lecture reviews direct-mapped caches and their conflict problem, then explains how set associativity gives a block multiple possible locations. Fully associative caches are presented as the extreme case with no index bits, maximum placement flexibility, and higher tag-comparison cost.

chapters.title: Cache block priorities: insertion, promotion, and eviction
chapters.summary: A set-associative cache is described as maintaining priorities for blocks in each set to decide what should be kept. The three main policy decisions are insertion on a miss, promotion on a hit, and eviction or replacement on a miss, with predictors estimating future locality and sometimes refetch cost.

chapters.title: Replacement policy options: random, FIFO, LRU, frequency, and hybrids
chapters.summary: Several replacement policies are introduced, including random replacement, first-in first-out, least recently used, not-most-recently-used, and frequency-based policies. The lecture stresses that replacement should depend on workload behavior and that real processors often use hybrid predictors rather than one fixed rule.

chapters.title: Cost of implementing true LRU and common approximations
chapters.summary: True LRU requires encoding the complete access order of all ways in a set, which grows factorially with associativity; a two-way set needs one bit, while a four-way set needs enough state for 4! orderings. Because true LRU is expensive and only an approximation of future locality, processors use simpler approximations such as not-MRU and hierarchical LRU-like schemes.

chapters.title: Example: LRU thrashing versus random replacement
chapters.summary: A cyclic reference pattern to five blocks in a four-way set demonstrates that LRU can produce a 0% hit rate when the working set of a set exceeds associativity. Random or hybrid policies can do better under thrashing, motivating sampling and meta-prediction to choose policies per set or globally.

chapters.title: Belady’s optimal replacement policy and its limitations
chapters.summary: Belady’s OPT policy evicts the block referenced furthest in the future and is optimal for minimizing miss rate under specific assumptions. The lecture warns that it is not necessarily optimal for execution time because misses have different costs, and that implementing or even simulating OPT requires future knowledge.

chapters.title: Write handling: dirty bits, write-through, write-back, and sector caches
chapters.summary: The tag store is extended with valid, replacement, and dirty or modified bits, leading to the trade-off between write-through and write-back caches. The lecture then distinguishes write-allocate from no-write-allocate policies and introduces sub-blocked or sector caches, where each sector has its own valid and dirty bits to avoid fetching or writing an entire block unnecessarily.

chapters.title: Instruction versus data caches: unified and split designs
chapters.summary: Unified caches allow dynamic sharing of capacity between instructions and data, avoiding underutilization from static partitioning. Split L1 instruction and data caches are usually preferred because instruction fetch and data access occur in different pipeline stages, while lower-level caches are usually unified.

chapters.title: Break announcement
chapters.summary: The instructor pauses the lecture for a short break and says the class will resume with more cache design decisions.

chapters.title: Multilevel cache management: L1 versus lower-level design constraints
chapters.summary: After the break, the lecture explains that different cache levels see different access streams and therefore need different designs and policies. L1 caches are latency-critical, small, low-associativity, and often access tags and data in parallel, while lower-level caches are larger, more associative, and may access tags before data to save energy.

chapters.title: Serial versus parallel access across cache levels
chapters.summary: The lecture compares accessing the next cache level only after a miss with speculatively accessing it in parallel with the previous level. Parallel access can reduce miss latency but wastes energy and bandwidth on hits, so processors may predict whether early next-level access is worthwhile.

chapters.title: Real processor cache hierarchies and software-visible cache movement
chapters.summary: Examples from Apple, AMD, and NVIDIA illustrate that modern processors devote large area to caches, including system-level caches, 3D-stacked cache, and GPU cache hierarchies. The lecture notes that some architectures expose cache bypassing or direct copy operations to software because cache placement is so important for performance.

chapters.title: Placement, eviction targets, and inclusive versus exclusive caches
chapters.summary: The lecture generalizes multilevel cache management to deciding which levels receive a block, which levels evicted blocks are written to, and whether levels can be bypassed. It defines inclusive, exclusive, and non-inclusive cache hierarchies and explains their trade-offs in space utilization and cache coherence complexity.

chapters.title: Cache performance parameters: size, block size, associativity, and critical word first
chapters.summary: Cache size, block size, and associativity are analyzed in terms of hit rate, hit latency, miss latency, bandwidth, and energy. Larger caches improve temporal locality until saturation, block size trades spatial locality against wasted space, critical-word-first refill reduces stall time, and associativity reduces conflicts at higher hardware cost.

chapters.title: Non-power-of-two associativity and practical layout choices
chapters.summary: The lecture explains that associativity does not have to be a power of two because cache ways are selected by tag matches rather than directly addressed. Real processors may use three-way, seven-way, twelve-way, or other associativities due to area, layout, and design constraints.

chapters.title: Q&A: whether modern CPUs can operate without caches
chapters.summary: A student asks whether processors today exist without caches; the instructor answers that modern CPUs essentially all have caches because locality is so important, though older systems or BIOS settings could sometimes disable caching. The discussion also mentions disabling prefetching as another possible system option.

chapters.title: Cache miss taxonomy and ways to reduce each miss type
chapters.summary: Cache misses are classified as compulsory, capacity, conflict, and coherence or communication misses. The lecture connects each type to possible remedies: prefetching or larger blocks for compulsory misses, more associativity or randomized indexing for conflict misses, and better working-set management for capacity misses.

chapters.title: Three goals of cache performance optimization
chapters.summary: The lecture summarizes the main performance goals as reducing miss rate, reducing miss latency or miss cost, and reducing hit latency or hit cost. It cautions that optimizing one metric can hurt another, for example by lowering miss rate while increasing hit latency or evicting more costly blocks.

chapters.title: Software locality optimization: loop interchange and tiling
chapters.summary: Software and compiler transformations are introduced as ways to improve cache behavior by restructuring data access patterns. Examples include loop interchange for column-major arrays and blocking or tiling for image filters and matrix multiplication so that smaller working sets fit in cache, scratchpad memory, or registers.

chapters.title: Data layout optimization: separating hot and cold fields
chapters.summary: A linked-list search example shows that cache space is wasted when rarely used fields share cache blocks with frequently accessed fields. The recommended transformation separates hot data such as keys and next pointers from cold data such as names or schools, raising the question of whether programmers, compilers, hardware, or AI should perform such restructuring.

chapters.title: Agenda: advanced caches and prefetching after cache basics
chapters.summary: The lecture opens with the plan to continue cache-performance topics, cover advanced cache mechanisms, and then introduce prefetching. The instructor also motivates architectural trade-offs with examples such as Cerebras wafer-scale processors and points to updated readings and upcoming topics.

chapters.title: Factors determining cache miss latency and miss cost
chapters.summary: The lecture reviews that a cache miss’s cost depends not only on where the block is found but also on whether the miss stalls the processor. It discusses latency variation from cache hierarchy level, DRAM row hits/conflicts, bank/rank/channel conflicts, queuing, local versus remote memory, criticality, and whether another block is evicted.

chapters.title: Memory-level parallelism and MLP-aware cache replacement
chapters.summary: Memory-level parallelism (MLP) is introduced as servicing multiple memory accesses concurrently, making isolated misses more costly than parallel misses. A loop example compares Belady’s optimal replacement, which minimizes miss count, with an MLP-aware policy that allows more misses but fewer stalls by retaining serially used blocks.

chapters.title: Predicting off-chip misses to overlap cache lookup and DRAM access
chapters.summary: A second latency-overlap example asks whether a predictor can identify accesses that will miss in on-chip caches and start the main-memory request early. The idea is to hide on-chip cache hierarchy latency on the critical path, while avoiding excessive bandwidth and energy waste from false predictions.

chapters.title: Victim caches and transition to multicore cache issues
chapters.summary: The instructor briefly introduces victim caches as a small structure that holds blocks evicted from a direct-mapped cache to reduce conflict misses, describing it as a low-cost form of associativity. The lecture then transitions to multicore systems, where cache and memory efficiency become more important because resources are shared across cores and threads.

chapters.title: Hardware-friendly cache compression with Base-Delta-Immediate compression
chapters.summary: Cache compression is motivated by common value patterns such as zeros, repeated values, narrow values, and pointers within nearby memory regions. Base-Delta-Immediate (BDI) compression is explained as storing a base plus small deltas, enabling fast decompression via parallel additions and achieving performance similar to much larger caches.

chapters.title: Industrial compressed caches in IBM enterprise processors
chapters.summary: The lecture shows IBM enterprise-class systems that use very large cache hierarchies and hardware compression units. IBM results illustrate that compression can provide performance gains comparable to doubling cache size, but at much lower area cost.

chapters.title: Private versus shared caches and shared-resource trade-offs
chapters.summary: The instructor compares private and shared caches as instances of the broader question of resource sharing. Shared caches improve utilization, avoid duplicate shared data, and reduce communication latency, but they also create contention, performance variability, loss of isolation, and possible unfairness among threads.

chapters.title: Cache partitioning for multicore fairness and quality of service
chapters.summary: A two-thread example shows how a streaming thread can evict the working set of another thread in a shared cache, causing severe slowdown. Cache partitioning, memory bandwidth partitioning, and related resource-management mechanisms are presented as ways to combine high utilization with controllability, fairness, and protection against performance attacks.

chapters.title: Definition and mechanisms of cache coherence
chapters.summary: Cache coherence is defined as ensuring that processors caching the same memory block see a consistent value after reads and writes. The lecture sketches broadcast/snooping coherence with invalidations and then directory-based coherence using per-block sharer bits and an exclusive state to reduce unnecessary communication.

chapters.title: Putting memory-system mechanisms together
chapters.summary: The instructor emphasizes that real memory-system design must consider cache coherence requests, processor and accelerator traffic, resource sharing and partitioning, prioritization, prefetching, energy, predictability, and bandwidth guarantees. Examples include graphics/display traffic requiring guaranteed bandwidth so that quality of service is maintained.

chapters.title: Break and transition to prefetching
chapters.summary: The class takes a short break and then resumes with the new topic of prefetching. The transition frames prefetching as another major memory-latency tolerance technique.

chapters.title: Definition, motivation, and correctness of prefetching
chapters.summary: Prefetching is defined as predicting addresses that will be needed and bringing their data closer to the processor before demand access. The lecture explains why prefetching can reduce or eliminate compulsory, capacity, conflict, and coherence misses, and why wrong prefetches usually do not affect correctness, though they can create security side channels.

chapters.title: Hardware prefetcher structure and the what/when/where/how questions
chapters.summary: A hardware prefetcher is shown monitoring cache access streams and issuing predicted requests. The instructor introduces the four central design questions: what addresses to prefetch, when to issue the request, where to place the data and prefetcher, and how the prefetcher is operated by hardware, software, or both.

chapters.title: Examples of predictable cache-block address patterns
chapters.summary: Several cache-block access streams are analyzed to show what makes an address pattern predictable: sequential streams, fixed strides, repeating delta sequences, repeating symbolic patterns, and recurring offsets within changing base regions. These examples motivate different prefetcher designs for streams, strides, delta correlation, and data-structure field accesses.

chapters.title: Timeliness and placement decisions for prefetches
chapters.summary: The lecture discusses the trade-off between issuing prefetches too early, which risks eviction or useless requests, and too late, which fails to hide latency. It also covers where to prefetch data in the hierarchy, how to treat prefetched blocks relative to demand-fetched blocks, and why predicted prefetch accuracy can guide replacement and insertion policies.

chapters.title: Software, hardware, and execution-based prefetching methods
chapters.summary: Three broad prefetching approaches are introduced: software prefetching by programmers or compilers, hardware prefetching via monitored access patterns, and execution-based prefetching through helper or assist threads. The instructor notes that software prefetching works best for regular patterns, while hardware and execution-based methods can address more dynamic behavior.

chapters.title: ISA prefetch instructions and limitations of compiler prefetching
chapters.summary: The x86 PREFETCH instruction is used as an example of an interface with locality hints whose actual behavior is chosen by the microarchitecture. The instructor explains that software prefetching is difficult because the compiler must know what will miss, how early to issue the instruction, and where to avoid cache pollution.

chapters.title: Streaming prefetchers and the increasing cost of cache misses
chapters.summary: Streaming prefetching is described as fetching cache blocks N+1, N+2, and beyond when block N is accessed, with possible prefetchers at multiple cache levels. The idea is tied to Norman Jouppi’s 1990 work on stream buffers and victim caches, and to the long-term growth in cache-miss cost measured in cycles and instructions.

chapters.title: Prefetcher metrics: accuracy, timeliness, coverage, bandwidth, and pollution
chapters.summary: The lecture defines accuracy as useful prefetches over sent prefetches, timeliness as how much latency is hidden, and coverage as prefetched misses over all misses. It also introduces memory-bandwidth consumption and cache pollution as crucial costs, emphasizing that optimizing all metrics simultaneously is difficult.

chapters.title: Efficiency benefits of runahead/Scout prefetching and prefetch throttling
chapters.summary: Data from Sun/Oracle systems shows that runahead execution, called Scout in those processors, can deliver performance comparable to much larger caches. The lecture then introduces prefetcher throttling, where inaccurate prefetchers are dialed down and accurate ones are made more aggressive, including an example of Pentium 4 locality-based prefetching.

chapters.title: Instruction-based and memory-region-based stride prefetchers
chapters.summary: Stride prefetching records the distance between consecutive accesses and predicts future accesses when the stride becomes stable. The lecture compares per-instruction stride detection using the program counter with memory-region-based stride detection, and discusses confidence counters and timeliness issues.

chapters.title: Delta-correlation and signature-based prefetchers for complex regular patterns
chapters.summary: For more complex regular patterns, the lecture explains how histories of recent strides or deltas can predict the next delta. Signature-based or delta-correlation prefetchers maintain path confidence and stop prefetching when confidence becomes too low.

chapters.title: Content-directed prefetching for pointer-rich data structures
chapters.summary: Content-directed prefetching scans the contents of a cache block and prefetches values that appear to be pointers. The instructor highlights its stateless nature, discusses the need for confidence mechanisms to avoid excessive useless prefetches, and notes that Apple has publicly known implementations vulnerable to attacks.

chapters.title: Pythia: reinforcement-learning-based data prefetching
chapters.summary: Prefetching is formulated as a reinforcement-learning problem where the prefetcher observes features of a memory request, chooses an offset action, receives rewards based on usefulness, timeliness, and bandwidth impact, and updates Q-values. The Pythia prefetcher uses hardware-friendly table lookups and configurable rewards, achieving strong performance and becoming a common open-source prefetching baseline.

chapters.title: Closing: next topics in prefetching and virtual memory
chapters.summary: The lecture ends by announcing that the next session will continue with more hardware prefetchers and then move to virtual memory, described as one of the most difficult parts of system design. The instructor closes with weekend remarks.

chapters.title: Administrative introduction and lecture roadmap
chapters.summary: The guest lecturer introduces their background, research interests in hardware–OS co-design, prefetching, and systems for robotics/physical AI. The lecture plan is to revisit prefetching, focus deeply on runahead execution, and later switch to virtual memory.

chapters.title: Recap: definition, purpose, and correctness of prefetching
chapters.summary: Prefetching is reviewed as fetching data before the program demands it in order to hide high memory latency. The lecturer emphasizes that prefetching is opportunistic and does not affect program correctness, unlike branch misprediction or other speculation that requires rollback.

chapters.title: Predicting complex access patterns with history and reinforcement learning
chapters.summary: The lecture revisits hard-to-predict patterns such as multiple strides, streams, linked data structures, dictionaries, and hash tables. It then summarizes path confidence-based lookahead prefetching and Pythia, which uses Q-learning to choose prefetch actions such as stride and lookahead distance based on program features and delayed rewards.

chapters.title: Multiple prefetchers and multicore prefetch coordination
chapters.summary: Modern processors use many prefetchers at different cache levels to cover streams, strides, and irregular patterns, but this increases complexity and bandwidth pressure. In multicore systems, many prefetchers can contend for shared cache, buses, DRAM banks, and memory bandwidth, so hierarchical control and fairness-aware coordination become important.

chapters.title: Usefulness prediction and cache insertion for prefetched blocks
chapters.summary: The lecturer describes work that predicts whether a prefetched block brought into the last-level cache will be useful. Useful predicted prefetches are inserted with higher priority, while likely useless prefetches are inserted with low priority so they do not displace demand-fetched cache blocks.

chapters.title: Definition of execution-based prefetching and thread-based pre-execution
chapters.summary: Execution-based prefetching pre-executes pieces of the program solely to generate future memory accesses. The lecture introduces speculative helper threads or nano-threads that can run on another core, another hardware thread context, or the same context to prefetch data or compute branch outcomes.

chapters.title: Motivation for runahead execution: full-window stalls in out-of-order cores
chapters.summary: Runahead execution is introduced through the problem of a long-latency cache miss at the head of the reorder buffer. Even if younger instructions can execute, they cannot retire, the instruction window fills, and the core stalls unless it has an impractically large window.

chapters.title: Mechanism of runahead execution with checkpointing and invalid results
chapters.summary: When the oldest instruction is a long-latency cache miss, the processor checkpoints architectural state and enters runahead mode. It speculatively executes future instructions to generate prefetches, marks unavailable long-latency values as invalid, then restores the checkpoint and resumes normal execution when the original miss returns.

chapters.title: Example and intuition: overlapping cache misses during runahead
chapters.summary: A timing example contrasts a perfect large-window processor, a small-window processor that stalls on each miss, and a small-window processor using runahead to issue a later load miss early. A restaurant analogy explains runahead as using the same chef/core to prepare future work while waiting for a long-latency soup/cache miss.

chapters.title: Benefits, limitations, performance, and industrial use of runahead
chapters.summary: Runahead is accurate because it follows the actual program path, can prefetch data and instructions, and can train history-based structures such as branch predictors and prefetchers. Its costs include extra power, dependence on branch prediction, inability to handle dependent cache misses without extensions, and limits from memory-level parallelism; results show it can let a 128-entry window approach the performance of a much larger window and was used or adapted in Sun Rock/Scout, IBM POWER6, and NVIDIA Denver.

chapters.title: Runahead extensions for pointer chasing and thesis-level conclusions
chapters.summary: The lecturer explains Onur Mutlu’s runahead extensions for pointer-intensive programs: value prediction can guess a missing load value when it is likely a pointer, enabling dependent future addresses to be computed and prefetched. The section concludes that runahead shifted thinking from simply building larger reorder buffers to exploiting existing cores for prefetching and inspired a broad research area.

chapters.title: Break, advice, and transition from prefetching to virtual memory
chapters.summary: The class takes a short break, followed by brief advice on resilience, passion, learning, and research. The lecturer points students to additional Carnegie Mellon and online materials on runahead execution and prefetching, then ends the prefetching portion and transitions to virtual memory.

chapters.title: Introduction to virtual memory and the illusion of ideal memory
chapters.summary: Virtual memory is introduced as a cornerstone of modern systems that lets programmers write loads and stores as if memory had infinite capacity, zero latency, zero cost, and infinite bandwidth. Hardware and the operating system map virtual addresses to physical addresses transparently, so programs do not manage physical memory directly.

chapters.title: Namespace isolation example: why programs should not choose physical locations
chapters.summary: Using two programs that both name a variable such as X[0], the lecturer shows why direct programmer-controlled physical addressing would allow accidental overwrites. Virtual memory provides per-process namespaces and a system-managed mapping so identical virtual names or addresses in different processes do not collide in physical memory.

chapters.title: Benefits of virtual memory and drawbacks of direct physical addressing
chapters.summary: The lecture lists virtual memory benefits: each process has a large independent virtual address space, code and data can be relocated anywhere in physical memory, processes are isolated, and sharing can be implemented by mapping different virtual addresses to the same physical frame. It contrasts this with systems using only physical addresses, where programmers must manage limited memory, relocation, concurrency, and sharing manually.

chapters.title: Address translation with pages, frames, page tables, and page faults
chapters.summary: Virtual memory works by splitting virtual address space into pages and physical memory into frames, usually 4 KiB in many systems, then storing virtual-page-to-physical-frame mappings in a page table. Physical memory can be viewed as a fully associative cache of disk pages; if a page is not resident, the operating system handles a page fault by bringing it from disk into memory and updating the mapping.

chapters.title: Worked example: translating virtual addresses using page table entries
chapters.summary: A numerical example uses a 2 GiB virtual address space, 128 MiB physical memory, and 4 KiB pages to split addresses into virtual page number, physical page number, and page offset. The lecturer stresses that the page offset is not translated, demonstrates concatenating the physical page number with the unchanged offset, and explains valid bits and the page table base register.

chapters.title: Challenge of page table size and multilevel page tables
chapters.summary: A flat page table for a 64-bit virtual address space would be impossibly large, especially per process, because programs usually use only a sparse subset of the virtual space. Multilevel hierarchical page tables allocate only needed lower-level tables, using upper-level entries as pointers; examples include two-level 32-bit x86 and four-level x86-64 page tables rooted at CR3.

chapters.title: Translation overhead, OS responsibilities, page fault handling, and DMA
chapters.summary: Because page tables reside in memory, address translation can require extra memory accesses before the actual data access, especially with multiple page-table levels. The OS maintains page tables, updates the page table base on context switches, handles minor and major page faults, chooses physical frames or evictions, and uses DMA engines to move pages between disk and memory without tying up the CPU.

chapters.title: Opening and recap of virtual memory address translation
chapters.summary: The lecture opens as the final class meeting and recaps virtual memory: each process has a private virtual address space, virtual pages map to physical frames through multi-level radix-tree page tables, and DMA can bring faulted-in data from disk without CPU involvement.

chapters.title: Page replacement with the clock algorithm
chapters.summary: When physical memory is full, the OS must evict a page to bring in new disk data. True LRU is too expensive at memory scale, so systems use approximations such as the clock/second-chance algorithm, treating physical memory as a cache for disk.

chapters.title: Memory protection, sharing, and page-level permissions
chapters.summary: Virtual memory isolates processes by ensuring each process can access only physical pages mapped in its page table, while still allowing sharing such as read-only library pages. Page-table entries store access-control bits for read, write, execute, user/supervisor, and sharing permissions, corresponding to privilege levels such as x86 rings.

chapters.title: x86 page-table-entry flags and hierarchical permissions
chapters.summary: The lecture examines 32-bit x86 page directory entries and page table entries, showing that upper-level entries point to lower-level tables while also carrying permission flags. Permissions can be combined across levels, so a flag at a higher level can constrain many lower-level 4 KB pages.

chapters.title: Security impact of flipping page-table bits with RowHammer
chapters.summary: The lecturer motivates why page-table protection bits are security-critical: if an attacker can flip bits in page tables, they may change user/supervisor permissions or physical page numbers. This introduces RowHammer as a DRAM reliability failure that became a system security vulnerability capable of privilege escalation.

chapters.title: RowHammer mechanism and disturbance kernel
chapters.summary: RowHammer repeatedly opens and closes DRAM rows so that neighboring victim rows suffer bit flips. A small x86 disturbance kernel uses repeated loads and CLFLUSH instructions to force memory accesses, avoid cache hits, and create row activations that induce errors.

chapters.title: Google RowHammer exploit using page-table spraying
chapters.summary: The Google Project Zero attack sprays physical memory with many page tables by mapping many objects, increasing the chance that RowHammer flips a useful page-table entry. By making a user-writable mapping point to another page table, the attacker can directly modify page tables and gain arbitrary memory access.

chapters.title: Hardware support for fast address translation
chapters.summary: The lecture shifts to how hardware performs virtual-to-physical translation at runtime. The memory management unit per core uses TLBs, page-walk caches, and a hardware page-table walker to avoid repeatedly traversing the full page table in memory.

chapters.title: TLB hierarchy and cache-like TLB lookup
chapters.summary: Modern processors use separate L1 instruction and data TLBs, often backed by a unified L2 TLB; misses fall through to hardware page-table walking. A TLB works like a cache for page-table entries, using virtual-page-number index and tag fields to return permissions and the physical frame number.

chapters.title: Hardware-managed versus software-managed TLB misses
chapters.summary: Hardware-managed TLBs use dedicated circuitry to walk page tables and refill TLBs transparently, making misses faster but fixing the OS–hardware page-table contract. Software-managed TLBs, as in some MIPS processors, trap to the OS for refill and replacement, enabling flexible page-table organizations but adding exception and context-switch overhead.

chapters.title: Multiple page sizes and L1 data TLB lookup
chapters.summary: Modern systems support multiple page sizes, such as 4 KB, 2 MB, and 1 GB, to reduce the number of mappings and increase TLB reach. The trade-offs include internal fragmentation and higher page-clearing latency, and L1 TLBs may probe separate structures in parallel because the page size is not known before translation.

chapters.title: L2 TLB support for multiple page sizes with pseudo-associativity
chapters.summary: A unified L2 TLB may store both 4 KB and 2 MB translations in one structure by probing sequentially under different page-size assumptions. This pseudo-associative design is simple but can increase hit and miss latency, motivating optimizations such as parallel lookups and page-size prediction.

chapters.title: Hardware page-table walkers and page-walk caches
chapters.summary: A hardware page-table walker is a per-core state machine that services outstanding TLB misses by generating the addresses needed for multi-level page-table traversal. Page-walk caches store intermediate page-table pointers so the walker can skip some memory accesses, improving performance while adding area, power, and flexibility costs.

chapters.title: Virtual versus physical cache access, synonyms, and homonyms
chapters.summary: The lecture discusses when translation occurs relative to L1 cache access and the complications of virtually addressed caches. Homonyms occur when the same virtual address maps to different physical addresses in different processes, while synonyms occur when different virtual addresses map to the same physical address, creating potential cache consistency problems.

chapters.title: Virtual memory overheads, research directions, and summary
chapters.summary: The lecturer surveys the evolution and cost of virtual memory, including OS allocation overheads for short-running workloads and translation overheads for irregular, long-running workloads. He summarizes research tools and ideas such as VICTIMA, hashed translation, and decoupled translation, then concludes that virtual memory provides capacity illusion, protection, sharing, and hardware–software co-design challenges for future large, heterogeneous, and virtualized systems.

chapters.title: Course epilogue opening and learning goals
chapters.summary: Mohammad thanks Constantinos, notes this is his last day at ETH but that he expects to attend the exam, and begins the course epilogue. He recalls the course goals: understanding principles and precedents, evaluating design trade-offs, implementing a simple processor, debugging systems, and developing out-of-the-box architectural thinking.

chapters.title: Recap of the computer architecture stack and main takeaways
chapters.summary: The epilogue reviews the course path from transistors and logic to ISAs, microarchitecture, execution paradigms, memory systems, and virtual memory. The main takeaways are that the covered concepts are used in real systems, apply broadly beyond computer architecture, and train students in critical trade-off analysis.

chapters.title: Educational philosophy: training the mind and accepting change
chapters.summary: Mohammad emphasizes that education is not just memorizing facts but training the mind to think, citing Einstein. He also uses George Bernard Shaw quotes to encourage constructive unreasonableness, openness to change, integrity of mind, and critical evaluation of existing mechanisms.

chapters.title: Future directions in computer architecture and Safari research themes
chapters.summary: The epilogue lists topics not fully covered and future challenges in performance, energy, reliability, security, accelerators, and processing-in-memory. Safari’s research themes are framed as robust architectures, energy-efficient memory-centric computing, low-latency and predictable systems, and data-driven/data-aware architectures for AI, genomics, medicine, and other data-intensive applications.

chapters.title: Final conclusion and exam wishes
chapters.summary: The course closes with the claim that future intelligent architectures should be data-centric, data-driven, and data-aware. Mohammad thanks the students, mentions upcoming problem-solving sessions and the August exam, and wishes everyone a good semester break.
